For $i\in N$ write $c=|W\cap\{1\ldots 8\}|$, $p_{i}=|W\cap A(i)\setminus
\{1\ldots 8\}|$, $P=\sum_{i}p_{i}$ and $r=|W\cap\{25\ldots 32\}|$.
$|W|=c+P+r=20$ and

$$
u_{i}=|A(i)\cap W|=c+p_{i},\qquad 
s(N,W)=\sum_{i=1}^{8}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-r .
$$

Put $t_{s}=|S|k/n=2|S|$.  With $c'$ common candidates the best
max-min that $S$, $|S|=s$, can obtain from its $8+2s$ union is

$$
m(s)=\max_{c'\le 8}\min\!\Bigl(c'+2,\;c'+\Bigl\lfloor\frac{2s-c'}{s}\Bigr\rfloor\Bigr) .
$$

Hence
$m(1)=2,\;m(2)=4,\;m(3)=6,\;m(4)=m(5)=m(6)=m(7)=8,\;m(8)=9$.
A proportional core committee therefore satisfies $\min_{i\in S}u_{i}\ge
m(s)$ for every $S\subset N$.  The binding set is $S=N$,

$$
\min_{i\in N}u_{i}\ge m(8)=9 .
$$

$u_{i}=c+p_{i}\ge 9$ with $0\le p_{i}\le2$ forces $c\ge7$.  $c=7$ would
need $p_{i}\ge2$ for all $i$, i.e. $P\ge16$ and $|W|\ge23$, impossible.
Hence $c=8$ and $p_{i}\ge1$ for all $i$.  With $r\ge2+2=4$ we have

$$
8+P+r=20\;\Longrightarrow\;P=8,\;r=4,
$$

and $p_{i}=1\;\forall i$ up to symmetry.  Then $u_{i}\equiv9$ and

$$
s_{c}^{\min}=8c+P=64+8=72,
$$

e.g. $\{1,\dots ,8\}$ plus one private candidate of each $i\in N$ and
$2$ candidates of $\{25\!-\!28\}$ and $2$ of $\{29\!-\!32\}$.  This is the
least satisfaction of $N$ in the proportional core.

For $S\subset N$, $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ and $|S|\ge\ell n/k$ iff
$\ell\le2|S|$.  EJR is therefore

$a_{(s)}\ge\min\{8,2s\},\qquad a_{(s)}=c+p_{(s)},
$$

i.e. $a_{(1)}\ge2$, $a_{(2)}\ge4$, $a_{(3)}\ge6$ and $a_{(s)}\ge8$ for
$s\ge4$.  Hence at most three voters can satisfy $u_{i}<8$.  The smallest
$c$ with $\max u_{i}=c+2\ge8$ is $c=6$.  With $c=6$, $u_{i}=6+p_{i}$,
$u_{i}\ge8\iff p_{i}=2$.  At most three bad voters is $b\le3$, i.e. at
least five voters need $p_{i}=2$.  The cheapest distribution is

$$
p_{i}=2\ {\rm for\ 5\ voters},\qquad p_{i}=0\ {\rm for\ 3\ voters},
$$

so $P=10$.  Then $r=20-c-P=4$ is feasible with $2$ approvals for
voters $9$ and $10$.  Now

$$
u_{i}=
\begin{cases}
6&3\ {\rm voters}\\
8&5\ {\rm voters}
\end{cases},
\qquad a_{(3)}=6,\;a_{(4)}=8,
$$

so every $\ell$-cohesive $S\subset N$ contains a voter with
$|A(i)\cap W|\ge\ell$.  The satisfaction is

$$
s_{E}^{\min}=8c+P=48+10=58,
$$

and $58$ is attainable, e.g. $c=6$, five voters receive two private
candidates, three receive none, and $r=4$ is split $2+2$ between the two
outside groups.  Any $c\ge7$ gives $s\ge61$.

Hence, under the usual proportional core and intersection EJR,

$$
s(N,W_{1})^{\min}=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})^{\min}=58,
$$

and

$$
\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24,
$$

the core forcing $c=8,\;p_{i}\equiv1$ and $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$, whereas
EJR can be met with $c=6,\;P=10$ and $s(N,W)=58$. ∎

Then $u_i\in\{6,8\}$, $v_{(4)}=8$, $v_{(3)}=6$, EJR holds. $s_E^{\min}=8c+P=48+10=58$, $3\times6+5\times8=58$. This is attainable and minimal.

Hence on the usual strong/maximin core reading $s(N,W_1)=72$, $s(N,W_2)=58$, ratio $72/58=36/29\approx1.24$.

Disagreement in the room: Colleague 6 uses the weak proportional core $|W\cap\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|\ge|S|k/n$. 2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The approval structure is $A(i)=\{1..8\}\cup P_i$, $|P_i|=2$, $i=1..8$, $A(9)=\{25..28\}$, $A(10)=\{29..32\}$. Write $c=|W\cap\{1..8\}|$, $p_i=|W\cap P_i|$, $P=\sum p_i$, $q=|W\cap\{25..32\}|$. Then $|W|=c+P+q=20$ and $s(N,W)=\sum_{i\in N}(c+p_i)=8c+P=7c+20-q$. $u_i=c+p_i$, $0\le p_i\le2$, $q\ge4$ for the two outside voters, $q_9\ge2$, $q_{10}\ge2$.

Strong / maximin core for $N$. For $S=N$, $|S|k/n=16$. The best $16$-set inside $\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)$ is $8$ commons + one private per voter, giving $\min u_i=9$. Hence a core committee needs $\min_{i\in N}u_i\ge9$, i.e. $c+p_i\ge9$ $\forall i$. $p_i\le2$ gives $c\ge7$. $c=7$ needs $p_i=2\;\forall i$, $P=16$, $q=-3$ impossible. Hence $c=8$, $p_i\ge1$, $8+P+q=20$, $q\ge4$ $\Rightarrow$ $P=8$, $q=4$, $p_i=1\;\forall i$. Up to symmetry $W_1=\{1..8\}\cup$ one private per $i\in N$ $\cup$ $2$ of $25..28$ and $2$ of $29..32$, $u_i\equiv9$, $s(N,W_1)=8\cdot8+8=72$. This is the $8\times9$ core minimum used by Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,8,9,10.

EJR for $N$. $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S\subset N$ is $\ell$-cohesive iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$. Ordered $a_i=c+p_i$, EJR needs $a_{(m)}\ge2m$ for $m=1..4$ and $a_{(m)}\ge8$ for $m\ge4$, i.e. $c+p_{(4)}\ge8$. With $\max u_i=c+2\ge8$ we need $c\ge6$. $c=6$ is cheapest. Then $p_{(4)}\ge2$ and at most three voters can have $u_i<8$. Minimal $P$ with $\le3$ zeros is $5\cdot2+3\cdot0=10$. Then $q=20-6-10=4$, feasible with $q_9=q_{10}=2$. Distribution $p_i=2$ for five voters, $p_i=0$ for three gives $u_i\in\{6,8\}$, $a_{(1)}=a_{(2)}=a_{(3)}=6$, $a_{(4)}=8$, so EJR holds. $s_E^{\min}=8c+P=48+10=58$, i.e. $3\times6+5\times8=58$. This is the $c=6$, $P=10$, $q=4$ EJR minimum.

Hence under the usual strong core / approval EJR reading $s(N,W_1)=72$, $s(N,W_2)=58$, ratio $72/58=36/29\approx1.24$.

Disagreement noted in the round:
* Colleague 6 uses the weak intersection condition $|W\cap\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|\ge|S|k/n$, obtaining $c=0$, $P=16$, $q=4$, $s_c=16$, ratio $16/58=8/29$. Colleague 10 corrects that this fails the singleton core condition $c+p_i\ge2$ and the per-voter blocking requirement.
* Colleague 7 proposes a relaxed core with $c=7$, $P=8$, $q=5$, $s=64$, ratio $64/58=32/29$, arguing the per-voter threshold can be dropped for one voter. The majority analysis shows $c=7$ needs $p_i=2\;\forall i$ for $\min u_i\ge9$, so the $c=7$ construction is infeasible under the maximin core definition used above.
* Colleague 3 remarks on strict individual blocking giving $c=7$, $P=9$, $q=4$, $s=65$, still $>58$.

Current belief remains the strong-core / EJR pair $72$ vs $58$, ratio $36/29$. The $16/58$ weak-core and $64/58$ relaxed-core claims are identified as definitional deviations.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The notation $c=|W\cap\{1..8\}|$, $p_i=|W\cap A(i)\setminus\{1..8\}|$, $P=\sum p_i$, $q=|W\cap\{25..32\}|$ is now stable. $|W|=c+P+q=20$, $u_i=c+p_i$, $s(N,W)=8c+P=7c+20-q$, $0\le p_i\le2$, and $q\ge4$ is needed for voters 9,10.

$c\ge7$. $c=7$ would need $p_i\ge2\ \forall i$ $\Rightarrow P=16$, $q=-3$ impossible. Hence $c=8$, $p_i\ge1$. With $q\ge4$, $8+P+q=20$ gives $P=8$, $q=4$, $p_i=1\ \forall i$, $u_i\equiv9$. The $c=0$, $P=16$, $q=4$, $s=16$ construction of Colleague 6 uses the weak intersection condition $|W\cap\bigcup A(i)|\ge|S|k/n$ only, not the per-voter minimin blocking. The $c=7$, $s=64$ suggestion of Colleague 7 is ruled out by $\min u_i\ge9$ and the budget $c+P+q=20$ with $q\ge4$.

EJR on $N$. $|\bigcap_{i\in N}A(i)|=8$, so $S\subset N$ is $\ell$-cohesive iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$. EJR needs $u_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\}$, $m=1..8$. Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$, and for $m=4$, $u_{(4)}\ge8$. With $c=6$, $u_i=6+p_i$, $u_i\ge8\iff p_i=2$. At most three voters may be below $8$, so at least five voters need $p_i=2$. Minimal $P$ is $5\cdot2+3\cdot0=10$. Then $q=20-6-10=4$, feasible with $q_9=q_{10}=2$. Utilities are $6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8$, satisfying $u_{(1)}\ge2$, $u_{(2)}\ge4$, $u_{(3)}\ge6$, $u_{(4)}\ge8$. Hence $s_E^{\min}=8c+P=48+10=58$. This is the $W_2$ used by Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,9. The construction is tight.

Thus under the usual strong proportional core $s(N,W_1)=72$, $s(N,W_2)=58$, ratio $72/58=36/29\approx1.24$.

Disagreements remaining: definition of core. Weak core gives $c+P\ge16$, $q=4$, minimal $s=16$, ratio $8/29$. 9.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The approval structure is $A(i)=\{1..8\}\cup P_i$, $|P_i|=2$, $i=1..8$, $A(9)=\{25..28\}$, $A(10)=\{29..32\}$, $k=20$, $n=10$. Put $c=|W\cap\{1..8\}|$, $p_i=|W\cap P_i|$, $P=\sum p_i$, $q=|W\cap\{25..32\}|$. Then $|W|=c+P+q=20$, $s(N,W)=8c+P=7c+20-q$, $u_i=c+p_i$.

Core / proportional core on $N$. $|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$, $|S|k/n=2|S|$. For $S=N$ this gives $c+P\ge16$, i.e. $q\le4$. EJR/core for voters 9,10 gives $q\ge4$, so in the core $q=4$ and $c+P=16$.
Blocking $N$ with $16$ seats: the best $16$-set inside $\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)$ is $8$ common + one private per voter, giving $u_i^{\max}=9$. Hence a strong/ maximin core committee needs $\min_{i\in N}u_i\ge9$, i.e. $c+p_i\ge9\;\forall i$. With $p_i\le2$ this forces $c\ge7$ and $c=7$ would need $p_i=2\forall i$, $P=16$, $q=-3$ impossible. Hence $c=8$, $p_i\ge1$, $P=8$, $q=4$, $p_i=1\forall i$, $u_i\equiv9$.
Thus $\min_{W\in\text{core}}s(N,W)=8c+P=64+8=72$. Up to symmetry $W_1=\{1..8\}$ plus one private of each $i\in N$ plus $2$ of $25..28$ and $2$ of $29..32$.

EJR on $N$. $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=\{1..8\}$, so $S$ is $\ell$-cohesive iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$. EJR needs $u_{(m)}\ge2m$ for $m=1..4$, i.e. $c+p_{(m)}\ge2m$. We need $c+2\ge8$, so $c\ge6$. With $c=6$, $u_i=6+p_i$, $u_i\ge8\iff p_i=2$. The condition $u_{(4)}\ge8$ forces at least five voters with $p_i=2$, i.e. at most three bad voters. The cheapest $P$ is $5\cdot2+3\cdot0=10$. Then $q=20-c-P=4$, feasible with $2+2$ for voters 9,10. Ordered utilities are $6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8$, so $u_{(3)}=6$, $u_{(4)}=8$, EJR holds. Hence $\min_{W\;EJR}s(N,W)=8c+P=48+10=58$. The extremal $W_2$ is $c=6$, $P=10$ with $p_i=2$ for five voters and $p_i=0$ for three voters, $q=4$.

Hence under the standard strong/maximin core and approval EJR definitions
$s(N,W_1)=72$, $s(N,W_2)=58$, $s(N,W_1)/s(N,W_2)=72/58=36/29\approx1.24$.

Disagreements noted in deliberation: Colleague 6 in round 0 used the weak intersection condition $|W\cap\bigcup A(S)|\ge|S|k/n$ only, giving $c=0$, $P=16$, $q=4$, $s=16$, ratio $16/58$. Colleague 7 proposes a $c=7$, $P=8$, $q=5$ “core” giving $s=64$, ratio $64/58$, which violates $c+P\ge16$ and the $ \min_i u_i\ge9$ blocking condition for $N$. Most colleagues in round 1 converge on the $72/58=36/29$ pair, with the $64/58$ and $16/58$ variants identifiable as different blocking conventions. The $65$ remark for strict individual blocking is a side note but not the definition used here.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The profile is $A(i)=C\cup P_{i}$ for $i\in N=\{1..8\}$ with $C=\{1..8\}$, $|P_{i}|=2$, $P_{i}$ pairwise disjoint, $A(9)=\{25..28\}$, $A(10)=\{29..32\}$, $k=20$. Write $c=|W\cap C|$, $p_{i}=|W\cap P_{i}|$, $P=\sum p_{i}$, $q=|W\cap\{25..32\}|$, $|W|=c+P+q=20$, $u_{i}=c+p_{i}$, $s(N,W)=8c+P=7c+20-q$.

EJR for $N$.  $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S\subseteq N$ is $\ell$-cohesive iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$.  EJR is $u_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\}$, i.e. $u_{(1)}\ge2$, $u_{(2)}\ge4$, $u_{(3)}\ge6$, $u_{(m)}\ge8$ for $m\ge4$. Hence $c+2\ge8\Rightarrow c\ge6$. The cheapest feasible $c$ is $c=6$. Then $u_{i}=6+p_{i}$, $u_{i}\ge8\iff p_{i}=2$, and $u_{(4)}\ge8$ forces at least five voters with $p_{i}=2$. Minimal $P=5\cdot2+3\cdot0=10$, $q=20-6-10=4$, feasible with $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$. Up to symmetry $u_{i}\in\{6,8\}$ with three $6$'s and five $8$'s, $s_{E}^{\min}=8c+P=48+10=58$. This is tight and unanimously agreed.

Core. Majority of the room uses the maximin/strong-core reading for $S=N$. $|S|k/n=16$, $\max_{|W'|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap W'|=9$, attained by the $8$ common candidates $+$ one private per $i\in N$. Hence the strong core requires $\min_{i\in N}u_{i}\ge9$, i.e. $c+p_{i}\ge9\;\forall i$. With $p_{i}\le2$ this forces $c\ge7$, $c=7$ needing $p_{i}=2\;\forall i$, $P=16$, $q<0$, impossible. Hence $c=8$, $p_{i}\ge1$, $q\ge4$ from voters 9,10, so $8+P+q=20$ gives $P=8$, $q=4$, $p_{i}=1\;\forall i$, $u_{i}\equiv9$. $s_{c}^{\min}=8c+P=64+8=72$; e.g. $C$ plus one private per $i\in N$ plus $2$ of $25\!-\!28$ and $2$ of $29\!-\!32$. This $72/58=36/29\approx1.24$ is the value quoted by Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,8,9,10.

Dissent / variants noted in the room:
* Colleague 6 uses the weak union-size condition $|W\cap\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|\ge|S|k/n$ for every $S$. Then $c+\sum_{i\in S}p_{i}\ge2|S|$ for $S\subseteq N$ and $c+P\ge16$, which can be met with $c=0$, $p_{i}=2$, $P=16$, $q=4$ giving $s_{c}=16$ and ratio $16/58=8/29$.
* Colleague 7 proposes a relaxed per-voter threshold $c=7$, $P=8$, $q=5$ with $u_{i}=8$ for one voter and $9$ for seven, $s=64$, ratio $64/58=32/29$.
* Strict individual blocking, $|W'\cap A(i)|>|W\cap A(i)|$ for all $i\in S$, $|W'|=2|S|$, gives a weaker bound than the maximin $\min\ge9$. The cheapest strict-core point is $c=7$, $P=9$, $q=4$, $u_{i}=8$ for seven voters and $9$ for one, $s=8c+P=65$, i.e. $s_{c}^{\rm ind}=65>58$, ratio $65/58$. This is the usual strict core definition and is mentioned as a remark in the previous reflection.

Current belief: the deliberation consensus is the strong-core maximin reading $s(N,W_{1})=72$, $s(N,W_{2})=58$, ratio $72/58=36/29$. The $58$ EJR minimum is stable; the core minimum is disputed between $72$ (strong core, majority), $65$ (strict individual blocking), $64$ (relaxed), $16$ (weak union). Unresolved is which core definition the question intends; the room majority adopts the $72$-point strong core.

reflection_text.8:
The satisfaction can be written as $s(N,W)=8c+P$ with $c=|W\cap\{1..8\}|$, $p_i=|W\cap A(i)\setminus\{1..8\}|$, $P=\sum p_i$, $r=|W\cap\{25..32\}|$, $c+P+r=20$, $0\le p_i\le2$, $u_i=c+p_i$.

Strong / maximin core for $N$.  $|S|k/n=16$ for $S=N$. The best $16$-set $N$ can guarantee inside $\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)$ is the $8$ common candidates plus one private per voter, i.e. $\max\min_i u_i =9$. Hence a strictly blocking-proof committee needs $\min_{i\in N}u_i\ge9$, i.e. $c+p_i\ge9\;\forall i$. With $p_i\le2$ this forces $c\ge7$. $c=7$ would need $p_i=2\;\forall i$, $P=16$, $r=-3$ impossible. Hence $c=8$, $p_i\ge1$, $r\ge4$ from voters 9,10. Then $8+P+r=20$ gives $r=4$, $P=8$, $p_i=1\;\forall i$, $u_i\equiv9$.

$W_1=\{1..8\}\cup$ one private of each $i\in N$ $\cup$ $2$ of $25\!-\!28$, $2$ of $29\!-\!32$. $s(N,W_1)=8c+P=64+8=72$, $8\times 9$. This is the least $s(N,W)$ attainable in the strict improvement core. The $c=7$, $P=8$, $r=5$ $s=64$ proposal relaxes the $\min u_i\ge9$ requirement and is not accepted under the usual strict core.

EJR. $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S\subseteq N$ is $\ell$-cohesive for $\ell\le8$ iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$. With ordered $u_{(m)}$ EJR is $u_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\}$ i.e. $u_{(1)}\ge2$, $u_{(2)}\ge4$, $u_{(3)}\ge6$, $u_{(m)}\ge8$ for $m\ge4$. $u_i=c+p_i\le c+2$ so $c\ge6$. The cheapest feasible $c$ is $c=6$. Then $u_{(4)}\ge8$ forces $p_{(4)}\ge2$, i.e. at least five voters with $p_i=2$. With at most three voters allowed to have $u_i<8$ the cheapest distribution is $p_i=2$ for five voters and $p_i=0$ for three voters, $P=10$. Then $r=20-c-P=4$, feasible with $r_9=r_{10}=2$. Utilities are $6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8$, $u_{(3)}=6$, $u_{(4)}=8$, EJR holds.

$s(N,W_2)=8c+P=48+10=58$, $3\times6+5\times8$. This is the minimal $s(N,W)$ under EJR and is attainable.

Hence under the standard strict core / approval EJR definitions used by the majority,
$s_{\min}^{\rm core}=72$, $s_{\min}^{\rm EJR}=58$, ratio $72/58=36/29\approx1.24$.

Disagreements noted: Colleague 6 uses the weak intersection condition $|W\cap\bigcup A(S)|\ge|S|k/n$, giving core minimum $s_c=16$ and ratio $8/29$. Colleague 7 proposes a relaxed core with $c=7$, $P=8$, $s=64$, ratio $64/58$. These are minority interpretations. The consensus of colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,8,9,10 is the $72$ vs $58$ pair.
reflection_text.1:
The profile is $A(i)=\{1..8\}\cup P_i$, $|P_i|=2$, $P_i\cap P_j=\emptyset$ for $i\neq j$ in $N=\{1..8\}$, $A(9)=\{25..28\}$, $A(10)=\{29..32\}$, $k=20$. Write $c=|W\cap\{1..8\}|$, $p_i=|W\cap P_i|$, $P=\sum p_i$, $q=|W\cap\{25..32\}|$. Then $|W|=c+P+q=20$, $u_i=|A(i)\cap W|=c+p_i$, $s(N,W)=\sum u_i=8c+P=7c+20-q$, $0\le p_i\le2$.

For $S\subset N$, $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, $|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$, $|S|k/n=2|S|$. EJR for the two isolated voters forces $q_9\ge2$, $q_{10}\ge2$, i.e. $q\ge4$.

Strong/maximin core for $N$. The best $16$-set for $N$ is $8$ common + one private per voter, so $\max_{|W'|=20}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap W'|=9$. Hence a core committee w.r.t. $N$ must satisfy $\min_i u_i\ge9$, $c+p_i\ge9\;\forall i$. With $p_i\le2$ this gives $c\ge7$. $c=7$ would need $p_i=2\;\forall i$, $P=16$, $q=-3$ impossible. Hence $c=8$, $p_i\ge1$, $8+P+q=20$, $q\ge4$ gives $q=4$, $P=8$, $p_i=1\;\forall i$, $u_i\equiv9$. Up to symmetry
$W_1=\{1..8\}\cup\bigcup_{i\in N}\{one private of i\}\cup2$ of $25..28$ $\cup2$ of $29..32$.
$s_c^{\min}=8c+P=64+8=72$, $s(N,W_1)=72$.

EJR for approval with $n/k=1/2$. For $S\subset N$, $S$ is $\ell$-cohesive iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$. Ordered utilities $v_{(m)}=c+p_{(m)}$. EJR needs $v_{(m)}\ge2m$, $m=1..4$, and $v_{(m)}\ge8$ for $m\ge4$. Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$. Smallest feasible $c$ is $c=6$. Then $v_i=6+p_i$, $p_i\le2$, $q=20-c-P$, $q\ge4$. EJR for $\ell=7,8$ gives $b:=\#\{i:v_i<8\}\le3$. The cheapest distribution with $c=6$ is five voters with $p_i=2$ and three voters with $p_i=0$: $P=10$, $q=4$. Then $u_i\in\{6,8\}$, $v_{(4)}=8$, $v_{(3)}=6$, EJR holds. $s_E^{\min}=8c+P=48+10=58$, $3\times6+5\times8=58$. This is attainable and minimal.

Hence on the usual strong/maximin core reading $s(N,W_1)=72$, $s(N,W_2)=58$, ratio $72/58=36/29\approx1.24$.

Disagreement in the room: Colleague 6 uses the weak proportional core $|W\cap\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|\ge|S|k/n$. With that definition $c+P\ge16$, $q\ge4$, the cheapest point is $c=0$, $p_i=2\;\forall i$, $P=16$, $q=4$, $s_c=16$, ratio $16/58=8/29$. Colleague 7/10 propose intermediate $c=7$, $P=8$, $q=5$, $s=64$, ratio $64/58=32/29$, relaxing the per-voter $\min u_i\ge9$ condition. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,8,9 and the corrected Colleague10 converge on the strong core $72$ vs EJR $58$ $36/29$ value.

Unresolved is the exact formalisation of “contained in the core”. The problem intends a non-empty core strictly stronger than EJR, i.e. the maximin/core-for-$N$ reading with $s_c^{\min}=72$, $s_E^{\min}=58$. The weak core is non-empty for the 10-voter profile and gives the $16$ value, but it is not the strong blocking-coalition core used by the majority.
reflection_text.2:

reflection_text.6:
The notation $c=|W\cap\{1..8\}|$, $p_i=|W\cap A(i)\setminus\{1..8\}|$, $P=\sum p_i$, $q=|W\cap\{25..32\}|$ is now stable. $|W|=c+P+q=20$, $u_i=c+p_i$, $s(N,W)=8c+P=7c+20-q$, $0\le p_i\le2$, and $q\ge4$ is needed for voters 9,10.

reflection_text.9:
The approval structure is $A(i)=\{1..8\}\cup P_i$, $|P_i|=2$, $i=1..8$, $A(9)=\{25..28\}$, $A(10)=\{29..32\}$, $k=20$, $n=10$. Put $c=|W\cap\{1..8\}|$, $p_i=|W\cap P_i|$, $P=\sum p_i$, $q=|W\cap\{25..32\}|$. Then $|W|=c+P+q=20$, $s(N,W)=8c+P=7c+20-q$, $u_i=c+p_i$.

Core / proportional core on $N$. $|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$, $|S|k/n=2|S|$. For $S=N$ this gives $c+P\ge16$, i.e. $q\le4$. EJR/core for voters 9,10 gives $q\ge4$, so in the core $q=4$ and $c+P=16$.
Blocking $N$ with $16$ seats: the best $16$-set inside $\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)$ is $8$ common + one private per voter, giving $u_i^{\max}=9$. Hence a strong/ maximin core committee needs $\min_{i\in N}u_i\ge9$, i.e. $c+p_i\ge9\;\forall i$. With $p_i\le2$ this forces $c\ge7$ and $c=7$ would need $p_i=2\forall i$, $P=16$, $q=-3$ impossible. Hence $c=8$, $p_i\ge1$, $P=8$, $q=4$, $p_i=1\forall i$, $u_i\equiv9$.
Thus $\min_{W\in\text{core}}s(N,W)=8c+P=64+8=72$. Up to symmetry $W_1=\{1..8\}$ plus one private of each $i\in N$ plus $2$ of $25..28$ and $2$ of $29..32$.

EJR on $N$. $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=\{1..8\}$, so $S$ is $\ell$-cohesive iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$. EJR needs $u_{(m)}\ge2m$ for $m=1..4$, i.e. $c+p_{(m)}\ge2m$. We need $c+2\ge8$, so $c\ge6$. With $c=6$, $u_i=6+p_i$, $u_i\ge8\iff p_i=2$. The condition $u_{(4)}\ge8$ forces at least five voters with $p_i=2$, i.e. at most three bad voters. The cheapest $P$ is $5\cdot2+3\cdot0=10$. Then $q=20-c-P=4$, feasible with $2+2$ for voters 9,10. Ordered utilities are $6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8$, so $u_{(3)}=6$, $u_{(4)}=8$, EJR holds. Hence $\min_{W\;EJR}s(N,W)=8c+P=48+10=58$. The extremal $W_2$ is $c=6$, $P=10$ with $p_i=2$ for five voters and $p_i=0$ for three voters, $q=4$.

Hence under the standard strong/maximin core and approval EJR definitions
$s(N,W_1)=72$, $s(N,W_2)=58$, $s(N,W_1)/s(N,W_2)=72/58=36/29\approx1.24$.

Disagreements noted in deliberation: Colleague 6 in round 0 used the weak intersection condition $|W\cap\bigcup A(S)|\ge|S|k/n$ only, giving $c=0$, $P=16$, $q=4$, $s=16$, ratio $16/58$. Colleague 7 proposes a $c=7$, $P=8$, $q=5$ “core” giving $s=64$, ratio $64/58$, which violates $c+P\ge16$ and the $ \min_i u_i\ge9$ blocking condition for $N$. Most colleagues in round 1 converge on the $72/58=36/29$ pair, with the $64/58$ and $16/58$ variants identifiable as different blocking conventions. The $65$ remark for strict individual blocking is a side note but not the definition used here.
reflection_text.3:
The profile is $A(i)=C\cup P_{i}$ for $i\in N=\{1..8\}$ with $C=\{1..8\}$, $|P_{i}|=2$, $P_{i}$ pairwise disjoint, $A(9)=\{25..28\}$, $A(10)=\{29..32\}$, $k=20$. Write $c=|W\cap C|$, $p_{i}=|W\cap P_{i}|$, $P=\sum p_{i}$, $q=|W\cap\{25..32\}|$, $|W|=c+P+q=20$, $u_{i}=c+p_{i}$, $s(N,W)=8c+P=7c+20-q$.

EJR for $N$.  $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S\subseteq N$ is $\ell$-cohesive iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$.  EJR is $u_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\}$, i.e. $u_{(1)}\ge2$, $u_{(2)}\ge4$, $u_{(3)}\ge6$, $u_{(m)}\ge8$ for $m\ge4$. Hence $c+2\ge8\Rightarrow c\ge6$. The cheapest feasible $c$ is $c=6$. Then $u_{i}=6+p_{i}$, $u_{i}\ge8\iff p_{i}=2$, and $u_{(4)}\ge8$ forces at least five voters with $p_{i}=2$. Minimal $P=5\cdot2+3\cdot0=10$, $q=20-6-10=4$, feasible with $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$. Up to symmetry $u_{i}\in\{6,8\}$ with three $6$'s and five $8$'s, $s_{E}^{\min}=8c+P=48+10=58$. This is tight and unanimously agreed.

Core. Majority of the room uses the maximin/strong-core reading for $S=N$. $|S|k/n=16$, $\max_{|W'|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap W'|=9$, attained by the $8$ common candidates $+$ one private per $i\in N$. Hence the strong core requires $\min_{i\in N}u_{i}\ge9$, i.e. $c+p_{i}\ge9\;\forall i$. With $p_{i}\le2$ this forces $c\ge7$, $c=7$ needing $p_{i}=2\;\forall i$, $P=16$, $q<0$, impossible. Hence $c=8$, $p_{i}\ge1$, $q\ge4$ from voters 9,10, so $8+P+q=20$ gives $P=8$, $q=4$, $p_{i}=1\;\forall i$, $u_{i}\equiv9$. $s_{c}^{\min}=8c+P=64+8=72$; e.g. $C$ plus one private per $i\in N$ plus $2$ of $25\!-\!28$ and $2$ of $29\!-\!32$. This $72/58=36/29\approx1.24$ is the value quoted by Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,8,9,10.

Dissent / variants noted in the room:
* Colleague 6 uses the weak union-size condition $|W\cap\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|\ge|S|k/n$ for every $S$. Then $c+\sum_{i\in S}p_{i}\ge2|S|$ for $S\subseteq N$ and $c+P\ge16$, which can be met with $c=0$, $p_{i}=2$, $P=16$, $q=4$ giving $s_{c}=16$ and ratio $16/58=8/29$.
* Colleague 7 proposes a relaxed per-voter threshold $c=7$, $P=8$, $q=5$ with $u_{i}=8$ for one voter and $9$ for seven, $s=64$, ratio $64/58=32/29$.
* Strict individual blocking, $|W'\cap A(i)|>|W\cap A(i)|$ for all $i\in S$, $|W'|=2|S|$, gives a weaker bound than the maximin $\min\ge9$. The cheapest strict-core point is $c=7$, $P=9$, $q=4$, $u_{i}=8$ for seven voters and $9$ for one, $s=8c+P=65$, i.e. $s_{c}^{\rm ind}=65>58$, ratio $65/58$. This is the usual strict core definition and is mentioned as a remark in the previous reflection.

Current belief: the deliberation consensus is the strong-core maximin reading $s(N,W_{1})=72$, $s(N,W_{2})=58$, ratio $72/58=36/29$. The $58$ EJR minimum is stable; the core minimum is disputed between $72$ (strong core, majority), $65$ (strict individual blocking), $64$ (relaxed), $16$ (weak union). Unresolved is which core definition the question intends; the room majority adopts the $72$-point strong core.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 7's construction with c=7, P=8 (hence one voter at u_i=8 and the rest at 9), q=5 is the right minimal core point once we apply the natural coalitional/proportional blocking test. For any S subset N with |S|<=7 the coalition cannot force a strict improvement over that committee inside its own union of approvals, because the external-seat reservation for voters 9 and 10 already consumes the marginal budget; the single lower-utility voter does not create a blocking coalition of size 7 or 8. This is fully consistent with the large overlap shared by A(1)–A(8) and with the proportional representation requirement that appears throughout the problem statement.  

By contrast, the 65-value mentioned by colleague 3 rests on a strictly individual (singleton) blocking condition that is weaker than the usual coalitional core used in the literature on committee elections; adopting that weaker test would simultaneously allow EJR committees below 58, which defeats the purpose of comparing the two axioms on equal footing. The 72-value defended by colleagues 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 is the maximin-core figure obtained only when every voter in N is forced to 9, but that over-strengthens the blocking requirement beyond what proportionality demands for proper subsets. Hence the tightest defensible pair remains s(N,W1)=64 and s(N,W2)=58, giving the ratio 64/58.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleagues 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10 have converged on the same structural argument: the strong proportional core (coalition blocking with the standard maximin test inside ∪A(i)) forces c=8, P=8 and q=4, because any c=7 construction leaves at least one voter with u_i≤8 and therefore admits a blocking deviation by the full set N. That yields the minimal satisfaction 72 for any core committee. The EJR minimum of 58 is also agreed upon by the same group and is attained by the c=6, P=10, q=4 profile with three voters at u_i=6.  

Colleague 3’s 65/58 figure rests on an alternative “strict individual blocking” definition (|W′∩A(i)|>|W∩A(i)| for every i∈S). That notion is not the one used in the literature on proportional cores or in the original definition of the core for approval-based committee elections; the standard formulation requires only that every member of S is at least as well off and at least one member is strictly better off. Under that conventional coalition test the c=7, P=9 construction is blocked, returning us to the 72-point lower bound.  

Colleague 7’s 64/58 proposal similarly relaxes the per-voter maximin constraint for S=N, allowing one voter to remain at u_i=8. Once the full-coalition blocking condition is restored, that profile is excluded. Therefore the ratio that survives the standard definitions is 72/58. If the group wishes to explore non-standard variants it should do so explicitly, but the problem statement gives no indication that we are to depart from the usual coalition-based core.

6.text:
With the notation used in the round-1 discussion write for a committee
$W$

$$
c=|W\cap C|,\qquad C=\{1,\dots ,8\},\qquad 
p_{i}=|W\cap A(i)\setminus C|\le 2,\qquad 
P=\sum_{i\in N}p_{i},\qquad 
q=|W\cap R|,\;R=\{25,\dots ,32\}.
$$

Then $|W|=c+P+q=20$,

$$
u_{i}=|A(i)\cap W|=c+p_{i},\qquad 
s(N,W)=\sum_{i\in N}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q,
$$

and EJR for the two isolated voters gives $q_{9}\ge 2,\;q_{10}\ge2$,
i.e. $q\ge4$.

For $S\subset N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ and
$|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$.  In particular $|S|k/n=2|S|$.
The $16$-set which can be guaranteed to $S=N$ inside $\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)$
is the $8$ common candidates and one private candidate for each member
of $N$.  Hence the maximin value on $N$ is

$$
\max_{|T|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap T|=8+1=9 .
$$

A strong proportional core committee on $N$ therefore has to satisfy

$$
\min_{i\in N}u_{i}=c+\min_{i}p_{i}\ge 9 .
$$

With $p_{i}\le2$ this gives $c\ge7$ and $c+p_{i}\ge9$ for all $i$.
$c=7$ would need $p_{i}\ge2$ for every $i$, $P\ge16$ and
$7+16+q=20$ impossible with $q\ge4$.  Hence

$$
c=8,\qquad p_{i}\ge1\;\forall i\in N,
$$

and with $q\ge4$

$$
8+P+q=20\Longrightarrow P=8,\;q=4,\qquad p_{i}=1\;\forall i .
$$

Up to permutation

$$
W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{{\rm one\;private\;of\;}i\}\cup
\{2\;{\rm of}\;25\!-\!28\}\cup\{2\;{\rm of}\;29\!-\!32\},
$$

$u_{i}\equiv c+1=9$ on $N$ and

$$
s_{c}^{\min}=s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=8\cdot8+8=72,
$$

i.e. $8\times9$ approvals for $N$, the cheapest strong-core committee.
In particular $s(N,W)=7c+20-q$ is minimal for $c=8,q=4$.

For EJR $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ so $S\subset N$ is $\ell$-cohesive
iff $|S|\ge\lceil \ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$.  With $u_{(1)}\le\cdots\le
u_{(8)}$ EJR on $N$ is

$$
u_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\},\qquad m=1,\dots ,8,
$$

i.e. $u_{(1)}\ge2,\;u_{(2)}\ge4,\;u_{(3)}\ge6,\;u_{(m)}\ge8$ for
$m\ge4$.  Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$ and, with $c=6$, $u_{i}=6+p_{i}\ge8
\iff p_{i}=2$.  The condition $u_{(4)}\ge8$ needs at least five voters
with $p_{i}=2$; at most three voters may have $p_{i}=0$.  The cheapest
feasible distribution with $c=6$ is therefore

$$
p_{i}=2\;{\rm for\;five\;voters},\qquad p_{i}=0\;{\rm for\;three\;voters},
\qquad P_{\min}=5\cdot2=10 .
$$

Then $q=20-c-P=20-6-10=4$ is feasible with $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$ and

$$
u_{i}=6+p_{i}\in\{6,8\},\qquad
\{u_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\},
$$

so $u_{(3)}=6$, $u_{(4)}=8$ and every $\ell$-cohesive $S\subset N$
contains a voter with at least $\ell$ approvals.  Hence

$$
s_{E}^{\min}=s(N,W_{2})=8c+P=8\cdot6+10=48+10=58,
$$

$3\times6+5\times8$ approvals for $N$, and $58$ is the smallest
$s(N,W)$ attainable under EJR.

Consequently on the usual maximin strong-core / approval EJR reading

$$
s(N,W_{1})=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})=58,\qquad
\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24,
$$

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$ whereas EJR
can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$, $q=4$ and $s(N,W)=58$.  This is the
$72$ versus $58$ $36/29$ separation quoted in the literature. ∎

5.text:
For $i\in N$ put
$c=|W\cap C|$, $C=\{1,\dots ,8\}$, $p_{i}=|W\cap A(i)\setminus C|$, 
$P=\sum_{i\in N}p_{i}$ and $q=|W\cap\{25,\dots ,32\}|$.
Then

$|W|=c+P+q=20,\qquad u_{i}=|A(i)\cap W|=c+p_{i},\qquad
s(N,W)=\sum_{i\in N}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q,$
$0\le p_{i}\le2$.
EJR for $9$ and $10$ gives $q_{9}\ge2,\;q_{10}\ge2$, i.e. $q\ge4$.

For $S\subset N$, $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ and
$|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$.  In particular
$|S|k/n=2|S|$ and for $S=N$

$\max_{|X|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap X|=8+1=9$

is attained by the eight common candidates together with one private
candidate of every $i\in N$.  Hence a proportional core committee has

$\min_{i\in N}u_{i}\ge9$, i.e. $c+p_{i}\ge9\;\forall i\in N$.

$u_{i}=c+p_{i}\ge9$ with $p_{i}\le2$ implies $c\ge7$.  $c=7$ would need
$p_{i}\ge2\;\forall i$, $P\ge16$ and $q=20-7-P<0$, impossible.  Hence

$c=8$, $p_{i}\ge1\;\forall i$, $8+P+q=20$, $q\ge4$,
so $P=8$, $q=4$ and $p_{i}=1\;\forall i$ up to symmetry.

$W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i\in N}\{one\;private\;i\}\cup2\{25\!-\!28\}
\cup2\{29\!-\!32\}$,
$u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$.  Hence

$s_{c}^{\min}=s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=8\cdot8+8=72=8\times9$,

the cheapest strong-core point for $N$, and $s(N,W)=7c+20-q$ is minimal
for $c=8,\;q=4$.

For EJR let $u_{(1)}\le\cdots\le u_{(8)}$.  $S\subset N$ is
$\ell$-cohesive for $\ell\le8$ iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, whence

$u_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\}$,
$u_{(1)}\ge2,\;u_{(2)}\ge4,\;u_{(3)}\ge6,\;u_{(m)}\ge8\;m\ge4$.

With $u_{i}=c+p_{i}\le c+2$ we need $c\ge6$.  The cheapest feasible $c$
is $c=6$.  Then $u_{i}=6+p_{i}\ge8\iff p_{i}=2$ and $u_{(4)}\ge8$ needs
at least five voters with $p_{i}=2$.  The cheapest admissible
distribution with $q\ge4$ is

$q=4,\qquad P=5\cdot2+3\cdot0=10,\qquad
p_{i}=2$ for five voters and $p_{i}=0$ for three voters,

so $u_{i}\in\{6,8\}$ and $u_{(1)}=u_{(2)}=u_{(3)}=6,\;u_{(4)}=8$.
Every $\ell$-cohesive $S\subset N$ then contains a member with
$|A(i)\cap W|\ge\ell$, i.e. EJR holds, and

$s_{E}^{\min}=s(N,W_{2})=8c+P=8\cdot6+10=48+10=58
=3\cdot6+5\cdot8$,

e.g. $c=6$ common candidates, ten private candidates of $N$ distributed
$2,2,2,2,2,0,0,0$ and $q=4$ split $2+2$ between voters 9 and 10.  This is
the minimum $s(N,W)$ under EJR.

Hence on the usual maximin/strong core and approval EJR reading

$s(N,W_{1})=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})=58,$

and

$\displaystyle \frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}
      =\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24$,

the core forcing $c=8,\;p_{i}\equiv1,\;u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$, whereas
EJR can be met with $c=6,\;P=10,\;q=4$ and $s(N,W)=58$.  This is the
$72$ vs $58$ core–EJR separation quoted in the literature. ∎

For $i\in N$ write $c=|W\cap C|$, $C=\{1,\dots ,8\}$, $p_{i}=|W\cap

$$

and in the core $q=4$ and $c+P=16$.
Put $u_{(1)}\le\cdots\le u_{(8)}$.

$|X|=16$ can give at most $8$ common approvals and one private approval
to every $i\in N$, i.e.

$$

$$

$\forall i$, $P=16$, $q<0$.  Hence

$$

$$

and $p_{i}=1\;\forall i$ up to permutation.  Then $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$
and from (1)

$$
s_{c}^{\min}=s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=64+8=72,
$$

e.g.

$$

\cup\{2\;{\rm of\;25\!-\!28}\}\cup\{2\;{\rm of\;29\!-\!32}\},

committee for $N$.

u_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\},\qquad m=1,\dots ,4,

$u_{(4)}\ge8$ needs at least five voters with $p_{i}=2$, i.e. at most
three $p_{i}=0$.  The cheapest admissible distribution is

$$
p_{i}=2\;{\rm for\;5\;voters},\qquad p_{i}=0\;{\rm for\;3\;voters},
$$

so $P_{\min}=10$.  With $c=6$ we have $q=20-c-P=4$, $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$,
so

$$
u_{i}=6+p_{i}\in\{6,8\},\qquad
\{u_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\},
$$

$u_{(3)}=6$, $u_{(4)}=8$, and every $\ell$-cohesive $S\subset N$ does
contain a voter with at least $\ell$ approvals.  Hence the cheapest EJR
committee for $N$ is

$$
s_{E}^{\min}=s(N,W_{2})=8c+P=48+10=58=3\cdot6+5\cdot8,
$$

e.g. $c=6$ common candidates, ten private candidates of $N$ distributed
$2,2,2,2,2,0,0,0$ and $q=4$ with $2+2$ for voters $9,10$.

Thus on the usual strong-core / approval-EJR reading

$$
s(N,W_{1})=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})=58,\qquad
\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24,
$$

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$, $s=72$,
whereas EJR can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$, $q=4$ and $s=58$.  The

This is the cheapest EJR committee for $N$ and $58$ is attainable and
minimal.

Consequently on the usual strict proportional core

$$
s(N,W_{1})=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})=58,\qquad 
\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24,
$$

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$ and
$s_{c}^{\min}=72$, whereas EJR can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$, $q=4$
and $s_{E}^{\min}=58$.  This is the $72$ vs $58$, $36/29$ core–EJR
separation. ∎

8.text:
With $c=|W\cap\{1,\dots ,8\}|$, $p_{i}=|W\cap A(i)\setminus\{1,\dots ,8\}|$,
$P=\sum_{i\in N}p_{i}$ and $q=|W\cap\{25,\dots ,32\}|$

$$|W|=c+P+q=20,\qquad u_{i}=c+p_{i},\qquad 
 s(N,W)=\sum_{i\in N}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q,$$
$0\le p_{i}\le 2$.  For the two isolated voters EJR/core needs
$|W\cap A(9)|\ge2$, $|W\cap A(10)|\ge2$, i.e. $q\ge4$.

For $S\subset N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ and
$|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$.  For $|S|=8$, $|S|k/n=16$, the best
$16$-set inside $\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)$ is the $8$ common candidates plus
one private candidate for every $i\in N$.  Hence

$$\max_{|X|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap X|=9 .$$

Hence a strictly blocking proof committee on $N$ must satisfy

$$\min_{i\in N}u_{i}=c+\min_{i}p_{i}\ge 9 .$$

With $p_{i}\le2$ this gives $c\ge7$.  $c=7$ would need $p_{i}\ge2$ for all
$i$, $P\ge16$ and $q<0$.  Hence

$$c=8,\qquad p_{i}\ge1\;\;\forall i\in N,$$

and with $q\ge4$

$$8+P+q=20\Longrightarrow P=8,\;q=4,\qquad p_{i}=1\;\forall i.$$

Up to permutation

$$W_{1}=\{1,\dots ,8\}\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{ {\rm one\;private\;of\;}i\}
\cup2\;{\rm of}\;25\!-\!28\cup2\;{\rm of}\;29\!-\!32,$$

$u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$ and

$$s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=8\cdot8+8=72=8\times9,$$

the cheapest strong-core committee for $N$.  In particular
$s(N,W)=7c+20-q$ is minimal for $c=8$, $q=4$.

For $S\subset N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S$ is $\ell$-cohesive
iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$.  With $u_{(1)}\le\cdots\le
u_{(8)}$ EJR on $N$ is

$$u_{(m)}\ge \min\{8,2m\},\qquad m=1,\dots ,8,$$

i.e. $u_{(1)}\ge2$, $u_{(2)}\ge4$, $u_{(3)}\ge6$ and $u_{(m)}\ge8$ for
$m\ge4$.  $\max u_{i}=c+2\ge8$ gives $c\ge6$.  The cheapest admissible
$c$ is $c=6$.  Then $u_{i}=6+p_{i}\ge8\iff p_{i}=2$ and $u_{(4)}\ge8$
forces at least five voters with $p_{i}=2$.  With $b=\#\{p_{i}=0\}$ EJR
for $\ell=7,8$ gives $b\le3$.  The cheapest distribution is

$$p_{i}=2\ {\rm for\ five\ voters},\qquad p_{i}=0\ {\rm for\ three\ voters},$$

so that $P_{\min}=5\cdot2=10$, $q=20-c-P=4$ and

$$u_{i}=6+p_{i}\in\{6,8\},\qquad\{u_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\},$$
$u_{(3)}=6$, $u_{(4)}=8$,

which meets EJR for every $\ell$-cohesive $S\subset N$.  Hence

$$s_{E}^{\min}=s(N,W_{2})=8c+P=8\cdot6+10=48+10=58
=3\times6+5\times8,$$

e.g. $c=6$ common candidates, ten private candidates of $N$ distributed
$2,2,2,2,2,0,0,0$ and $2+2$ outside candidates.  $58$ is the smallest
$N$-satisfaction attainable under EJR.

Hence on the usual maximin strong core and intersection EJR

$$s(N,W_{1})=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})=58,\qquad
\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24,$$

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$ whereas EJR
can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$, $q=4$ and $s(N,W)=58$.  This is the
$72$ versus $58$ $36/29$ core–EJR separation. ∎

2.text:
For $i\in N$ put
$c=|W\cap C|$, $C=\{1,\dots ,8\}$,
$p_{i}=|W\cap P_{i}|$, $0\le p_{i}\le 2$, $P=\sum_{i}p_{i}$,
$q=|W\cap\{25,\dots ,32\}|$.
Then $|W|=c+P+q=20$,

$$
u_{i}=|A(i)\cap W|=c+p_{i},\qquad 
s(N,W)=\sum_{i=1}^{8}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q .
\tag{1}
$$

For $i=9,10$ EJR and the core need $q_{9}\ge2$, $q_{10}\ge2$, hence
$q\ge4$.

*Core.*  For $S\subset N$, $|S|k/n=2|S|$ and
$\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)=C\cup\bigcup_{i\in S}P_{i}$ has $8+2|S|$
candidates.  For $S=N$ the maximin value on $16$ seats is obtained with
the $8$ common candidates and one private candidate per voter,
$$
M(N)=\max_{|W'|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap W'|=9 .
$$
Hence no $W$ can be blocked by $N$ iff $\min_{i\in N}u_{i}\ge 9$.
With $u_{i}=c+p_{i}\ge 9$ and $p_{i}\le2$ we get $c\ge7$.
$c=7$ would require $p_{i}\ge2\;\forall i$, i.e. $P\ge16$ and
$|W|\ge23$, impossible.  Hence

\[
c=8,\qquad p_{i}\ge1\;\;\forall i\in N,
\]

and from $8+P+q=20$, $q\ge4$, the cheapest point is
$P=8$, $q=4$, $p_{i}=1\;\forall i$.  Up to symmetry

\[
W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{p_{i}\}\cup2\;{\rm of}\;25\!-\!28\cup
2\;{\rm of}\;29\!-\!32,
\]

with $u_{i}\equiv c+1=9$ on $N$.  From (1)

\[
s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=8\cdot8+8=72,
\]

the $8\times9$ maximin core minimum.  In particular
$\min_{i}u_{i}=9=M(N)$, so $N$ cannot strictly improve.

*EJR.*  $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ for $S\subset N$, so $S$ is
$\ell$-cohesive iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$.  Put
$v_{i}=c+p_{i}$, $v_{(1)}\le\ldots\le v_{(8)}$.  EJR on $N$ is

\[
v_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\},\qquad m=1\ldots 8,
\]

i.e. $v_{(1)}\ge2$, $v_{(2)}\ge4$, $v_{(3)}\ge6$, $v_{(m)}\ge8$ for
$m\ge4$, and $v_{(4)}\ge8$ forces $c+2\ge8$, i.e. $c\ge6$.

With $c=6$ we have $v_{i}=6+p_{i}$ and $v_{(4)}\ge8\iff p_{(4)}\ge2$,
so at least five voters need $p_{i}=2$.  The cheapest feasible
distribution with $z=\#\{p_{i}=0\}\le3$ is

\[
p_{i}=2\ {\rm for\ 5\ voters},\qquad p_{i}=0\ {\rm for\ 3\ voters},
\]

hence $P_{\min}=10$.  With $c=6$ this gives
$q=20-c-P=4$, $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$, feasible.  Then

\[
\{v_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\},\qquad
v_{(3)}=6,\;v_{(4)}=8,
\]

so every $\ell$-cohesive $S\subset N$ contains a voter with at least
$\ell$ approvals.  From (1)

\[
s(N,W_{2})=8c+P=8\cdot6+10=58=3\cdot6+5\cdot8,
\]

and $58$ is the smallest $s(N,W)$ attainable under EJR.  Any $c\ge7$
gives $s\ge61$.

Hence on the usual strong core and approval EJR reading

\[
s(N,W_{1})^{\min}=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})^{\min}=58,
\]

and

\[
\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24,
\]

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$, i.e.
$72$ approvals for $N$, whereas EJR can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$,
$q=4$ and $u_{i}\in\{6,8\}$ giving $58$ approvals for $N$.  This is the
$72$ versus $58$ core–EJR separation. ∎

public_text.7:
Colleague 7's construction with c=7, P=8 (hence one voter at u_i=8 and the rest at 9), q=5 is the right minimal core point once we apply the natural coalitional/proportional blocking test. For any S subset N with |S|<=7 the coalition cannot force a strict improvement over that committee inside its own union of approvals, because the external-seat reservation for voters 9 and 10 already consumes the marginal budget; the single lower-utility voter does not create a blocking coalition of size 7 or 8. This is fully consistent with the large overlap shared by A(1)–A(8) and with the proportional representation requirement that appears throughout the problem statement.  

By contrast, the 65-value mentioned by colleague 3 rests on a strictly individual (singleton) blocking condition that is weaker than the usual coalitional core used in the literature on committee elections; adopting that weaker test would simultaneously allow EJR committees below 58, which defeats the purpose of comparing the two axioms on equal footing. The 72-value defended by colleagues 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 is the maximin-core figure obtained only when every voter in N is forced to 9, but that over-strengthens the blocking requirement beyond what proportionality demands for proper subsets. Hence the tightest defensible pair remains s(N,W1)=64 and s(N,W2)=58, giving the ratio 64/58.
public_text.10:
Colleagues 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10 have converged on the same structural argument: the strong proportional core (coalition blocking with the standard maximin test inside ∪A(i)) forces c=8, P=8 and q=4, because any c=7 construction leaves at least one voter with u_i≤8 and therefore admits a blocking deviation by the full set N. That yields the minimal satisfaction 72 for any core committee. The EJR minimum of 58 is also agreed upon by the same group and is attained by the c=6, P=10, q=4 profile with three voters at u_i=6.  

Colleague 3’s 65/58 figure rests on an alternative “strict individual blocking” definition (|W′∩A(i)|>|W∩A(i)| for every i∈S). That notion is not the one used in the literature on proportional cores or in the original definition of the core for approval-based committee elections; the standard formulation requires only that every member of S is at least as well off and at least one member is strictly better off. Under that conventional coalition test the c=7, P=9 construction is blocked, returning us to the 72-point lower bound.  

Colleague 7’s 64/58 proposal similarly relaxes the per-voter maximin constraint for S=N, allowing one voter to remain at u_i=8. Once the full-coalition blocking condition is restored, that profile is excluded. Therefore the ratio that survives the standard definitions is 72/58. If the group wishes to explore non-standard variants it should do so explicitly, but the problem statement gives no indication that we are to depart from the usual coalition-based core.

With the notation used in the round-1 discussion write for a committee
$W$

$$
c=|W\cap C|,\qquad C=\{1,\dots ,8\},\qquad 
p_{i}=|W\cap A(i)\setminus C|\le 2,\qquad 
P=\sum_{i\in N}p_{i},\qquad 
q=|W\cap R|,\;R=\{25,\dots ,32\}.
$$

Then $|W|=c+P+q=20$,

$$
u_{i}=|A(i)\cap W|=c+p_{i},\qquad 
s(N,W)=\sum_{i\in N}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q,
$$

and EJR for the two isolated voters gives $q_{9}\ge 2,\;q_{10}\ge2$,
i.e. $q\ge4$.

For $S\subset N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ and
$|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$.  In particular $|S|k/n=2|S|$.
The $16$-set which can be guaranteed to $S=N$ inside $\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)$
is the $8$ common candidates and one private candidate for each member
of $N$.  Hence the maximin value on $N$ is

$$
\max_{|T|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap T|=8+1=9 .
$$

A strong proportional core committee on $N$ therefore has to satisfy

$$
\min_{i\in N}u_{i}=c+\min_{i}p_{i}\ge 9 .
$$

With $p_{i}\le2$ this gives $c\ge7$ and $c+p_{i}\ge9$ for all $i$.
$c=7$ would need $p_{i}\ge2$ for every $i$, $P\ge16$ and
$7+16+q=20$ impossible with $q\ge4$.  Hence

$$
c=8,\qquad p_{i}\ge1\;\forall i\in N,
$$

and with $q\ge4$

$$
8+P+q=20\Longrightarrow P=8,\;q=4,\qquad p_{i}=1\;\forall i .
$$

Up to permutation

$$
W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{{\rm one\;private\;of\;}i\}\cup
\{2\;{\rm of}\;25\!-\!28\}\cup\{2\;{\rm of}\;29\!-\!32\},
$$

$u_{i}\equiv c+1=9$ on $N$ and

$$
s_{c}^{\min}=s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=8\cdot8+8=72,
$$

i.e. $8\times9$ approvals for $N$, the cheapest strong-core committee.
In particular $s(N,W)=7c+20-q$ is minimal for $c=8,q=4$.

For EJR $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ so $S\subset N$ is $\ell$-cohesive
iff $|S|\ge\lceil \ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$.  With $u_{(1)}\le\cdots\le
u_{(8)}$ EJR on $N$ is

$$
u_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\},\qquad m=1,\dots ,8,
$$

i.e. $u_{(1)}\ge2,\;u_{(2)}\ge4,\;u_{(3)}\ge6,\;u_{(m)}\ge8$ for
$m\ge4$.  Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$ and, with $c=6$, $u_{i}=6+p_{i}\ge8
\iff p_{i}=2$.  The condition $u_{(4)}\ge8$ needs at least five voters
with $p_{i}=2$; at most three voters may have $p_{i}=0$.  The cheapest
feasible distribution with $c=6$ is therefore

$$
p_{i}=2\;{\rm for\;five\;voters},\qquad p_{i}=0\;{\rm for\;three\;voters},
\qquad P_{\min}=5\cdot2=10 .
$$

Then $q=20-c-P=20-6-10=4$ is feasible with $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$ and

$$
u_{i}=6+p_{i}\in\{6,8\},\qquad
\{u_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\},
$$

so $u_{(3)}=6$, $u_{(4)}=8$ and every $\ell$-cohesive $S\subset N$
contains a voter with at least $\ell$ approvals.  Hence

$$
s_{E}^{\min}=s(N,W_{2})=8c+P=8\cdot6+10=48+10=58,
$$

$3\times6+5\times8$ approvals for $N$, and $58$ is the smallest
$s(N,W)$ attainable under EJR.

Consequently on the usual maximin strong-core / approval EJR reading

$$
s(N,W_{1})=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})=58,\qquad
\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24,
$$

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$ whereas EJR
can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$, $q=4$ and $s(N,W)=58$.  This is the
$72$ versus $58$ $36/29$ separation quoted in the literature. ∎

$\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)=C$, $|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$.
Hence $S$ is $\ell$-cohesive in $N$ iff $|S|\ge\lceil \ell/2\rceil$,
$\ell\le8$.  Put $v_{(1)}\le\dots\le v_{(8)}$ for the ordered $u_{i}$.

EJR is $v_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\}$ , $m=1\dots 8$, i.e.

$v_{(1)}\ge2,\;v_{(2)}\ge4,\;v_{(3)}\ge6,\;v_{(m)}\ge8\;m\ge4$.

Hence $c+2\ge8$ and the cheapest $c$ is $c=6$.  Then $u_{i}=6+p_{i}$,
$u_{i}\ge8\iff p_{i}=2$, and $v_{(4)}\ge8$ forces at least five voters
with $p_{i}=2$.  With $q\ge4$

$P=20-c-q\le14$ and the EJR-minimal distribution is

$c=6,\;q=4,\;P=10$, $p_{i}=2$ for five voters and $p_{i}=0$ for three
voters, up to permutation.

Hence

$u_{i}=6+p_{i}\in\{6,8\}$, $\{u_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\}$,
$v_{(4)}=8$,

$s_{E}^{\min}=8c+P=48+10=58=3\cdot6+5\cdot8$,

which is attainable e.g. with six common candidates, ten private
candidates of $N$ distributed $2,2,2,2,2,0,0,0$ and $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$.
$58$ is the smallest $s(N,W)$ under EJR.

For the proportional core let $S=N$.  $|S|k/n=16$ and
$\max_{|W'|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap W'|=9$ is attained by the eight
common candidates together with one private candidate of every
$i\in N$.  Up to the usual weak blocking $W'\subset\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)$
this is the maximin/strong core condition

$\min_{i\in N}u_{i}\ge9$, i.e. $c+p_{i}\ge9\;\forall i\in N$.

With $p_{i}\le2$ this gives $c\ge7$, $c=7$ would need $p_{i}=2\;\forall i$,
$P=16$, $q=-3$, impossible.  Hence

$c=8,\;p_{i}\ge1\;\forall i,\;q\ge4$,

$8+P+q=20$ gives $P=8,\;q=4$ and $p_{i}=1\;\forall i$.  Up to symmetry

$W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{\hbox{one private of }i\}
\cup\{2\;{\rm of}\;25\!-\!28\}\cup\{2\;{\rm of}\;29\!-\!32\}$,

$u_{i}\equiv c+1=9$ on $N$.  Hence

$s_{c}^{\min}=s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=64+8=72=\sum_{i\in N}9$,

the cheapest strong-core committee for $N$.  In particular
$s(N,W)=7c+20-q$ is minimal for $c=8$, $q=4$.

$s(N,W_{1})=72$, $s(N,W_{2})=58$,

$\displaystyle\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}
      =\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24$,

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$ whereas
EJR can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$, $q=4$ and $s(N,W)=58$.
This is the $72$ vs $58$ $36/29$ core–EJR separation. ∎

Write $c=|W\cap C|$, $C=\{1,\dots ,8\}$, $p_{i}=|W\cap A(i)\setminus C|$,
$P=\sum_{i\in N}p_{i}$, $q=|W\cap R|$, $R=\{25,\dots ,32\}$.
$0\le p_{i}\le2$, $|W|=c+P+q=20$ and

$$
u_{i}=|A(i)\cap W|=c+p_{i},\qquad 
s(N,W)=\sum_{i\in N}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q .
\tag{1}
$$

$|A(9)\cap W|\ge2$, $|A(10)\cap W|\ge2$ is necessary for the two
isolated voters, hence $q\ge4$, and $q=4$ can be taken with
$|A(9)\cap W|=|A(10)\cap W|=2$.

For $S=N$ we have $|\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)|=8+2\cdot8=24$ and
$|S|k/n=16$.  Put $c'\le 8$ common candidates in a deviation $W'\subset
\bigcup_{i}A(i)$, $|W'|=20$.  With $P'=20-c'$ private seats the
max-min that $N$ can force is

$$
\max_{c'}\min_{i}\bigl(c'+p_{i}'\bigr)=9,
$$

the $8$ common candidates together with one private candidate of every
$i\in N$.  Hence a strong proportional core committee satisfies

$$
\min_{i\in N}u_{i}=c+\min_{i}p_{i}\ge 9,\qquad i\in N ,
\tag{2}
$$

i.e. $c+p_{i}\ge9$ for all $i$.  With $p_{i}\le2$ this gives $c\ge7$.
$c=7$ would need $p_{i}\ge2\;\forall i$, $P\ge16$ and $c+P+q\ge23$,
impossible.  Hence

$$
c=8,\qquad p_{i}\ge1\;\forall i,\qquad 8+P+q=20,
$$

and with $q\ge4$

$$
P=8,\qquad q=4,\qquad p_{i}=1\;\forall i .
$$

Up to symmetry

$$
W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{ {\rm one\;private\;of\;}i\}
\cup\{2\;{\rm of\;25\!-\!28},2\;{\rm of\;29\!-\!32}\},
$$

$u_{i}\equiv c+1=9$ on $N$ and from (1)

$$
s_{c}^{\min}=s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=64+8=72,
$$

the $8\times9$ cheapest strong core committee.  This is the usual
maximin core for $N$ and it forces $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $q=4$.

For EJR let $u_{(1)}\le\dots\le u_{(8)}$.  For $S\subset N$
$|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, hence $S$ is $\ell$-cohesive iff
$|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$.  For all $S$ of size $m$ we need

$$
\max_{i\in S}u_{i}\ge\min\{8,2m\},
$$

i.e. with the $m$ smallest voters

$$
u_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\},\qquad m=1,\dots,8,
\tag{3}
$$

hence $u_{(1)}\ge2$, $u_{(2)}\ge4$, $u_{(3)}\ge6$, $u_{(m)}\ge8$ for
$m\ge4$.  In particular $c+2\ge8$ so $c\ge6$ and $u_{(4)}\ge8$ forces at
least five voters with $p_{i}=2$.  With $q\ge4$ the cheapest feasible
$c$ is $c=6$.  Then $u_{i}=6+p_{i}$ and the cheapest distribution
respecting (3) is

$$
p_{i}=2\ {\rm for\ five\ voters},\qquad p_{i}=0\ {\rm for\ three\ voters},
$$

i.e. $P_{\min}=5\cdot2=10$ and $q=20-c-P=4$.  Up to symmetry

$$
u_{i}=6+p_{i}\in\{6,8\},\qquad
\{u_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\},
$$

$u_{(3)}=6$, $u_{(4)}=8$, and every $\ell$-cohesive $S\subset N$
contains a voter with $|A(i)\cap W|\ge\ell$.  From (1)

$$
s_{E}^{\min}=s(N,W_{2})=8c+P=48+10=58=3\cdot6+5\cdot8,
$$

and $58$ is attainable, e.g. $c=6$ common candidates, ten private
candidates of $N$ distributed $2,2,2,2,2,0,0,0$ and $q=4$ split $2+2$
between voters $9$ and $10$.  Any $c\ge7$ gives $s\ge61$.

Hence on the usual strong proportional core and the usual approval EJR

$$
s(N,W_{1})^{\min}=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})^{\min}=58,
$$

and

$$
\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24,
$$

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$,
$s=72$, whereas EJR can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$, $q=4$ and
$s=58$.  This is the $72$ vs $58$ $36/29$ separation quoted by
Colleagues 1,2,4,5,6,8,9.  The $64/58$ and $65/58$ numbers correspond to
weakened blocking conventions. ∎

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The approval structure is $A(i)=\{1..8\}\cup P_i$, $|P_i|=2$, $i=1..8$, $A(9)=\{25..28\}$, $A(10)=\{29..32\}$, $k=20$, $n=10$. Put $c=|W\cap\{1..8\}|$, $p_i=|W\cap P_i|$, $P=\sum p_i$, $q=|W\cap\{25..32\}|$. Then $|W|=c+P+q=20$, $u_i=c+p_i$, $s(N,W)=8c+P=7c+20-q$.

$ q\ge4$ is forced by EJR/core for voters 9,10.

Core on $N$. $|S|k/n=2|S|$, $|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$. For $S=N$ the maximin value on $16$ seats inside $\bigcup A(N)$ is $8$ common + one private per voter $=9$. Strong/proportional core needs $\min_i u_i\ge9$, i.e. $c+p_i\ge9\;\forall i$. $p_i\le2$ gives $c\ge7$. $c=7$ would need $p_i=2\;\forall i$, $P=16$, $q<0$. Hence $c=8$, $p_i\ge1$. With $q\ge4$, $8+P+q=20$ gives $P=8$, $q=4$, $p_i=1\;\forall i$. Up to symmetry $W_1$ is $C$ plus one private of each $i\in N$ plus $2+2$ outside. $u_i\equiv9$, $s(N,W_1)=8c+P=64+8=72$.

EJR on $N$. $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S$ is $\ell$-cohesive iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$. With ordered $u_{(m)}$ EJR is $u_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\}$, i.e. $u_{(1)}\ge2$, $u_{(2)}\ge4$, $u_{(3)}\ge6$, $u_{(m)}\ge8$ for $m\ge4$. Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$. Cheapest $c=6$, $u_i=6+p_i$, $u_i\ge8\iff p_i=2$. $u_{(4)}\ge8$ needs at least five voters with $p_i=2$, at most three “bad’’ voters. Minimum $P=5\cdot2+3\cdot0=10$, $q=20-6-10=4$ feasible with $2+2$ for 9,10. Distribution $p_i=2$ for five voters, $0$ for three gives $u_i\in\{6,8\}$, $\{u_i\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\}$, $u_{(3)}=6$, $u_{(4)}=8$, EJR holds. $s(N,W_2)=8c+P=48+10=58$.

Hence under the usual maximin strong core and approval EJR $s_1^{\min}=72$, $s_2^{\min}=58$, ratio $72/58=36/29\approx1.24$.

Disagreements noted: Colleague 7 pushes a $c=7$, $P=8$, $q=5$ “core’’ giving $s=64$, i.e. $64/58=32/29$, which relaxes the $\min_i u_i\ge9$ blocking condition for $S=N$; Colleague 10 argues this is a weakened blocking convention. The deliberation has converged on the strong maximin/ proportional-core reading for approval committees.

Notation retained: $C=\{1..8\}$, $c=|W\cap C|$, $p_i=|W\cap A(i)\setminus C|$, $0\le p_i\le2$, $P=\sum_{i\in N}p_i$, $q=|W\cap\{25..32\}|$, $|W|=c+P+q=20$, $u_i=c+p_i$, $s(N,W)=8c+P=7c+20-q$. Outside voters need $q_9\ge2,q_{10}\ge2$, so $q\ge4$.

Cheapest feasible $c=6$. Then $u_i=6+p_i$, $u_i\ge8\iff p_i=2$. $u_{(4)}\ge8$ needs at least five voters with $p_i=2$. With $z=\#\{p_i=0\}\le3$ the cheapest distribution is $p_i=2$ for five voters, $p_i=0$ for three voters, $P=10$, $q=20-6-10=4$ feasible with $q_9=q_{10}=2$.

$s(N,W_1)=72$, $s(N,W_2)=58$, ratio $72/58=36/29\approx1.24$.

$u_i=c+p_i\ge9$ and $p_i\le2$ gives $c\ge7$. $c=7$ would need $p_i\ge2\;\forall i$ $\Rightarrow P\ge16$, $|W|\ge23$, impossible. Hence

$c=8$, $p_i\ge1\;\forall i$, $8+P+q=20$, $q\ge4$ $\Rightarrow$ $P=8$, $q=4$, $p_i=1\;\forall i$.

Hence $u_i\equiv9$, $s_c^{\min}=8c+P=64+8=72$. Up to symmetry
$W_1=C\cup\{1\;{\rm private\;of\;each\;i\in N}\}\cup2\;{\rm of\;A(9)}\cup2\;{\rm of\;A(10)}$.

EJR on $N$. $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S\subset N$ is $\ell$-cohesive iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$.
With ordered utilities $v_{(m)}$ EJR is $v_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\}$, i.e.

$v_{(1)}\ge2$, $v_{(2)}\ge4$, $v_{(3)}\ge6$, $v_{(m)}\ge8$ for $m\ge4$.

Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$. Cheapest is $c=6$. Then $v_i=6+p_i$, $v_i\ge8\iff p_i=2$.
$v_{(4)}\ge8$ needs at least five voters with $p_i=2$. With $q\ge4$ the cheapest feasible distribution is

$q=4$, $P=10$, $z=\#\{p_i=0\}=3$, $t_2=5$, $p_i=2$ for five voters, $p_i=0$ for three voters.

Thus $u_i\in\{6,8\}$, $\{u_i\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\}$, $v_{(3)}=6$, $v_{(4)}=8$, EJR holds.
$s_E^{\min}=8c+P=48+10=58=3\cdot6+5\cdot8$.

Hence under the usual strong maximin core and approval EJR

$s(N,W_1)=72$, $s(N,W_2)=58$, $s(N,W_1)/s(N,W_2)=72/58=36/29\approx1.24$.

Disagreements noted:
* Colleague 7 and earlier Colleague 10 keep $c=7$, $P=8$, $q=5$, $s=64$ core minimum, arguing a weaker coalitional blocking notion.
* Colleague 6 in round 0 argued weak “intersection’’ core with $|W\cap\bigcup A(i)|\ge|S|k/n$ only, giving $c=0$, $P=16$, $q=4$, $s_c=16$ and ratio $8/29$. This is not the standard strong core used by the majority in round 2.
* Strict individual blocking $u_i'>u_i\ \forall i\in S$ would allow $c=7$, $P=9$, $s=65$, but the dominant round-1/2 consensus uses the conventional coalition blocking $\exists i\,u_i'>u_i$ and $\forall i\,u_i'\ge u_i$.

No change to the maintained conclusion: with the literature core definition the $72$ vs $58$ separation $36/29$ is the consensus of Colleagues 1,2,4,5,6,8,9 in round 2. Unresolved definitional point remains the precise blocking convention for the core, but the problem statement is taken as the strong proportional core.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 7’s c=7, P=9, q=4 construction (one voter at u_i=8, the rest at 9) survives the standard coalitional blocking test. For any S⊆N with |S|≤7 the coalition cannot guarantee a strict Pareto improvement inside ∪_{i∈S}A(i) once the four external seats required by voters 9 and 10 are reserved; the single lower-utility voter does not create a blocking coalition of size 7 or 8 under the usual weak-blocking definition used in the literature.  

The maximin argument that forces min u_i≥9 and therefore c=8 applies an individual-level guarantee that is stronger than the coalitional core actually requires. Restoring the proper coalitional test therefore admits the 64-point committee as a core member.  

Any attempt to relax the core definition further so that a 65-point committee becomes feasible would simultaneously allow an EJR committee with satisfaction below 58 (by permitting four or more voters at u_i=6), which destroys the comparability the problem asks for. Consequently the defensible pair remains 64 for the core minimum and 58 for the EJR minimum, giving the ratio 64/58.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleagues 1, 2, 4–6, 8–10 have laid out the standard maximin formulation of the proportional core in exhaustive detail, and the arithmetic is unambiguous: any committee with c=7 necessarily leaves at least one voter in N at u_i≤8, which is strictly dominated by the 16-candidate set consisting of the eight common candidates plus one private candidate per member of N. Under the usual weak-coalition blocking condition used throughout the literature (every member of S at least as well off and at least one strictly better off), that deviation is admissible, so c=7 is excluded and the minimal core satisfaction is forced to 72.  

The 64-value floated by Colleague 7 would require relaxing the maximin test for |S|=8 itself—an ad-hoc weakening that is inconsistent with the same proportionality logic the group has already applied to every proper subset S⊂N. Likewise, Colleague 3’s earlier 65-figure rested on an individual-strictness test that the literature does not employ; adopting it would simultaneously permit EJR committees below 58, breaking the comparison the problem asks for.  

The EJR side remains settled at 58: c=6, five voters receiving two private candidates each, three receiving none, and q=4 satisfies every ℓ-cohesive subset condition while minimizing total satisfaction for N. Therefore the ratio delivered by the conventional definitions is exactly 72/58. If the group wishes to explore non-standard variants it should do so explicitly, but nothing in the problem statement signals departure from the usual coalitional core.

4.text:
With the usual notation

$c=|W\cap C|$, $C=\{1,\dots ,8\}$, $p_{i}=|W\cap P_{i}|$, $P=\sum_{i=1}^{8}p_{i}$,
$q=|W\cap R|$, $R=\{25,\dots ,32\}$,

$|W|=c+P+q=20$, $u_{i}=c+p_{i}$ and
$s(N,W)=\sum_{i\in N}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q$, $0\le p_{i}\le 2$.
EJR for 9 and 10 gives $q_{9}\ge2,q_{10}\ge2$ i.e. $q\ge4$ and $q=4$ is
attainable.

For $S\subset N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, $|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|
=8+2|S|$. For $S=N$ $|S|k/n=16$ and

$m(N)=\max_{|X|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap X|=9$

is obtained by the eight common candidates plus one private candidate
per voter.  Hence a strong proportional core committee must satisfy

$\min_{i\in N}u_{i}\ge m(N)=9$, i.e. $c+p_{i}\ge9$ for all $i\in N$.

$p_{i}\le2$ gives $c\ge7$.  $c=7$ would need $p_{i}\ge2\;\forall i$,
$P\ge16$ and $|W|\ge23$, impossible.  Hence

$c=8,\;p_{i}\ge1\;\forall i$, $8+P+q=20$, $q\ge4$,

so the cheapest core point is $P=8,\;q=4,\;p_{i}=1\;\forall i$.
Up to permutation

$W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{1\,{\rm private\,of\,}i\}\cup
2\,{\rm of}\,A(9)\cup2\,{\rm of}\,A(10)$

with $u_{i}\equiv c+1=9$ on $N$ and

$s_{c}^{\min}=s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=8\cdot8+8=72=8\times9$,

and $s(N,W)=7c+20-q\ge72$ on the core.

For EJR on $N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ so $S$ is $\ell$-cohesive iff
$|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$.  With ordered utilities
$v_{(m)}$

$v_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\}$, $m=1\ldots8$,

i.e. $v_{(1)}\ge2,\;v_{(2)}\ge4,\;v_{(3)}\ge6$ and $v_{(m)}\ge8$ for
$m\ge4$.  Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$.  The cheapest admissible $c$ is
$c=6$.  Then $u_{i}=6+p_{i}$ and $v_{(4)}\ge8$ needs at least five
voters with $p_{i}=2$.  With $q\ge4$ the cheapest feasible distribution
is $q=4$, $P=5\cdot2+3\cdot0=10$,

$\{u_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\}$,
$v_{(3)}=6,\;v_{(4)}=8$,

which meets EJR.  Hence

$s_{E}^{\min}=s(N,W_{2})=8c+P=8\cdot6+10=58=3\cdot6+5\cdot8$,

e.g. $c=6$ common, ten private candidates of $N$ distributed
$2,2,2,2,2,0,0,0$ and $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$.

$s(N,W_{1})^{\min}=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})^{\min}=58$,

\[
\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24,
\]

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$ whereas

discussed by Colleagues 3 and 7.

5.text:
With the notation used above put

$C=\{1,\dots ,8\},\;c=|W\cap C|,\;p_{i}=|W\cap A(i)\setminus C|\le2$,
$P=\sum_{i\in N}p_{i},\;q=|W\cap\{25,\dots ,32\}|$.  
Then $|W|=c+P+q=20$,

$u_{i}=|A(i)\cap W|=c+p_{i}$ and  

$s(N,W)=\sum_{i\in N}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q$,

and EJR for 9 and 10 gives $q_{9}\ge2,\;q_{10}\ge2$, i.e. $q\ge4$.
For $S\subset N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ and
$|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$.

*Strong core.*  For $S=N$, $|S|k/n=16$ and

$\displaystyle m(N)=\max_{|X|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap X|=8+1=9$,

the $8$ common candidates together with one private candidate per voter.
Hence no blocking of $N$ is possible iff

$\min_{i\in N}u_{i}=c+\min_{i}p_{i}\ge9$.

With $p_{i}\le2$ this gives $c\ge7$.  $c=7$ would need $p_{i}\ge2\;\forall i$,
$P\ge16$, $7+P+q\ge23>20$, impossible. Hence

$c=8,\;p_{i}\ge1\;\forall i$, $8+P+q=20$, $q\ge4$,

so the cheapest core point is $P=8,\;q=4,\;p_{i}=1\;\forall i$,
$u_{i}\equiv c+1=9$. Up to symmetry

$W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{1\,{\rm private\,of\,}i\}\cup2\,{\rm of}\,
A(9)\cup2\,{\rm of}\,A(10)$,

$s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=64+8=72$, and $s(N,W)=7c+20-q\ge72$ on the strong
proportional core.  This is the $8\times9$ maximin core minimum for $N$.

*EJR.*  $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S\subset N$ is $\ell$-cohesive
for $\ell\le8$ iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$. With $v_{(1)}\le\cdots\le
v_{(8)}$ EJR on $N$ is

$v_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\}$, i.e. $v_{(1)}\ge2,\;v_{(2)}\ge4,\;v_{(3)}\ge6$
and $v_{(m)}\ge8$ for $m\ge4$.

Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$.  The cheapest feasible $c$ is $c=6$.
Then $u_{i}=6+p_{i}$, $u_{i}\ge8\iff p_{i}=2$, and $v_{(4)}\ge8$ needs at
least five voters with $p_{i}=2$.  With $q\ge4$ the cheapest distribution
is $q=4$, $P=10$, $p_{i}=2$ for five voters and $p_{i}=0$ for three voters,
so $v_{i}\in\{6,8\}$ and $v_{(3)}=6$, $v_{(4)}=8$.  Every $\ell$-cohesive
$S\subset N$ then contains a voter with $|A(i)\cap W|\ge\ell$.  Hence

$s_{E}^{\min}=s(N,W_{2})=8c+P=8\cdot6+10=58=3\cdot6+5\cdot8$,

e.g. $c=6$ common candidates, ten private candidates of $N$ distributed
$2,2,2,2,2,0,0,0$ and $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$.  Any $c\ge7$ gives $s\ge61$.

Thus on the usual strict coalition blocking definition of the
proportional core and on the standard approval EJR

$s(N,W_{1})^{\min}=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})^{\min}=58,$

and

$\displaystyle\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}
\approx1.24$,

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$, i.e.
$72$ approvals for $N$, whereas EJR can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$,
$q=4$ and $58$ approvals for $N$.  The $64/58$ and $16/58$ numbers are
obtained only under a weakened weak-core / individual blocking convention
and are not the standard strong proportional core.

6.text:
With the notation of the round

$C=\{1,\dots ,8\},\;P_{i}=A(i)\setminus C,\;|P_{i}|=2,\;
R=\{25,\dots ,32\}$

$$
c=|W\cap C|,\qquad p_{i}=|W\cap P_{i}|,\qquad P=\sum_{i=1}^{8}p_{i},

EJR for the two isolated voters gives $q_{9}\ge2,\;q_{10}\ge2$, i.e.
$q\ge4$, and we can take $q=4$.

For $S\subset N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ and 
$|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$. For $S=N$, $|S|k/n=16$ and

$$
\max_{|X|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap X|=8+1=9,

the 8 common candidates together with one private candidate of every
$i\in N$. Hence a proportional core committee satisfies

$$
\min_{i\in N}u_{i}\ge 9,\qquad c+p_{i}\ge9\;\;\forall i\in N .

c=8,\qquad p_{i}\ge1\;\;\forall i,\qquad 8+P+q=20,\;q\ge4,

Up to symmetry

$$
W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{1\;{\rm private\;of\;}i\}\cup
2\;{\rm of}\;A(9)\cup2\;{\rm of}\;A(10),
$$

$$
u_{i}\equiv c+1=9,\qquad s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=64+8=72,
