and $s(N,W)=7c+20-q\ge72$ on the strong proportional core.

For EJR on $N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S$ is $\ell$-cohesive
iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$. With $v_{(1)}\le\cdots\le
v_{(8)}$

$$
v_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\},\qquad 
v_{(1)}\ge2,\;v_{(2)}\ge4,\;v_{(3)}\ge6,\;v_{(m)}\ge8\;(m\ge4).
$$

Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$. The cheapest $c$ is $c=6$. Then
$v_{i}=6+p_{i}$ and $v_{(4)}\ge8$ needs at least five voters with
$p_{i}=2$. The cheapest feasible distribution with $q\ge4$ is
$q=4$, $P=10$, $z=\#\{p_{i}=0\}=3$, $t_{2}=5$,

$$
p_{i}=2\;{\rm for\;5\;voters},\qquad p_{i}=0\;{\rm for\;3\;voters},
$$

so that

$$
u_{i}=6+p_{i}\in\{6,8\},\quad\{u_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\},
$$

$v_{(3)}=6$, $v_{(4)}=8$ and every $\ell$-cohesive $S\subset N$
contains a voter with $|A(i)\cap W|\ge\ell$. Hence

$$
s_{E}^{\min}=8c+P=8\cdot6+10=48+10=58=3\cdot6+5\cdot8,
$$

e.g. $c=6$ common candidates, ten private candidates of $N$ distributed
$2,2,2,2,2,0,0,0$ and $q=4$ split $2+2$ between voters 9 and 10.

Thus on the usual maximin strong core and approval EJR

$$
s(N,W_{1})^{\min}=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})^{\min}=58,
$$

and

$$
\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24,
$$

the core forcing $c=8,\;p_{i}\equiv1,\;u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$,
$s=72$, whereas EJR can be met with $c=6,\;P=10,\;q=4$ and
$s(N,W)=58$. This is the $72$ vs $58$, $36/29$ core–EJR separation.

9.text:
Put $C=\{1,\dots ,8\}$, $P_{i}=A(i)\setminus C$, $|P_{i}|=2$, $R=\{25,\dots ,
32\}$ and for a $k=20$ committee $W$

$$
c=|W\cap C|,\qquad p_{i}=|W\cap P_{i}|,\qquad P=\sum_{i=1}^{8}p_{i},
\qquad q=|W\cap R|,
$$

$0\le p_{i}\le2$, $|W|=c+P+q=20$,

$$
u_{i}=|A(i)\cap W|=c+p_{i},\qquad 
s(N,W)=\sum_{i=1}^{8}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q .
$$

EJR/core for the isolated voters gives $|W\cap A(9)|\ge2$,
$|W\cap A(10)|\ge2$, hence $q\ge4$ and we may take $q=4$.

For $S\subset N$, $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ and
$|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$.  In particular for $S=N$

$$
|W\cap\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)|=c+P\ge16 ,
$$

and the maximin value attainable inside $\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)$ on
$16$ seats is the $8$ common candidates plus one private candidate per
voter,

$$
M(N)=\max_{|X|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap X|=8+1=9 .
$$

Hence a strong proportional core committee satisfies

$$
\min_{i\in N}u_{i}=c+\min_{i}p_{i}\ge M(N)=9,
\qquad c+p_{i}\ge9\;\;\forall i\in N .
$$

$p_{i}\le2$ gives $c\ge7$ and $c=7$ would need $p_{i}\ge2\;\forall i$,
$P\ge16$, $7+P+q>20$.  Hence

$$
c=8,\qquad p_{i}\ge1\;\forall i,\qquad 8+P+q=20,\;q\ge4,
$$

and the cheapest point is $P=8$, $q=4$, $p_{i}=1\;\forall i$.  Up to
permutation

$$
W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{1\;{\rm private\;of\;}i\}
\cup2\;{\rm of}\;A(9)\cup2\;{\rm of}\;A(10),
$$

$$
u_{i}\equiv c+1=9,\qquad 
s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=64+8=72,
$$

and $s(N,W)=7c+20-q\ge72$ on the strong core.  This is the $8\times9$
cheapest core committee for $N$.

For EJR, $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S\subset N$ is $\ell$–cohesive
iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$.  With $v_{(1)}\le\cdots\le
v_{(8)}$ the EJR condition on $N$ is

$$
v_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\},\qquad1\le m\le8,
$$

i.e. $v_{(1)}\ge2$, $v_{(2)}\ge4$, $v_{(3)}\ge6$ and $v_{(m)}\ge8$ for
$m\ge4$.  Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$, and $v_{(4)}\ge8$ forces at least
five voters with $p_{i}=2$.  The cheapest feasible $c$ is $c=6$.
Then $u_{i}=6+p_{i}$ and the cheapest EJR distribution with $q\ge4$ is

$$
q=4,\qquad P=5\cdot2+3\cdot0=10,\qquad 
p_{i}=2\;{\rm for\;5\;voters},\;p_{i}=0\;{\rm for\;3\;voters},
$$

so that

$$
\{u_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\},\qquad v_{(3)}=6,\;v_{(4)}=8,
$$

and every $\ell$–cohesive $S\subset N$ contains a voter with at least
$\ell$ approvals.  Hence

$$
s(N,W_{2})=8c+P=8\cdot6+10=48+10=58=3\cdot6+5\cdot8,
$$

attainable e.g. with $c=6$ common candidates, ten private candidates of
$N$ distributed $2,2,2,2,2,0,0,0$ and $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$.  This is the
minimum $s(N,W)$ under approval EJR, and any $c\ge7$ gives $s\ge61$.

Hence on the usual maximin strong core and approval EJR

$$
s(N,W_{1})^{\min}=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})^{\min}=58,
$$

$$
\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24,
$$

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$ and
$s_{c}^{\min}=72$, whereas EJR can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$, $q=4$
and $s_{E}^{\min}=58$.  This is the $72$ vs $58$, $36/29$ core–EJR
separation. The $c=7$, $P=8$, $q=5$ and the $c=0$, $P=16$ variants are
obtained only under a weakened individual or intersection blocking
convention and are not the standard strong proportional core. ∎

8.text:
With the usual notation

$C=\{1,\dots ,8\},\;P_{i}=A(i)\setminus C,\;|P_{i}|=2,\;R=\{25,\dots ,32\}$

$c=|W\cap C|,\;p_{i}=|W\cap P_{i}|,\;P=\sum_{i=1}^{8}p_{i},\;q=|W\cap R|$,

$|W|=c+P+q=20$,

$$
u_{i}=|A(i)\cap W|=c+p_{i},\qquad 
s(N,W)=\sum_{i=1}^{8}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q,
$$
$0\le p_{i}\le 2$.  EJR for $9,10$ gives $q_{9}\ge2,q_{10}\ge2$, i.e. $q\ge4$
and $q=4$ can be attained with $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$.

For $S\subset N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ and 
$|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$.  In particular $|S|k/n=2|S|$.
For $S=N$

$$
\max_{|X|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap X|=8+1=9
$$

is obtained by the eight common candidates and one private candidate
per voter. Hence a strong proportional core committee satisfies

$$
\min_{i\in N}u_{i}=c+\min_{i}p_{i}\ge 9 .
$$

$p_{i}\le2$ gives $c\ge7$. $c=7$ would need $p_{i}\ge2\;\forall i$, $P\ge16$
and $|W|\ge23$, impossible. Hence

$$
c=8,\qquad p_{i}\ge1\;\forall i,\qquad 8+P+q=20,\;q\ge4,
$$

so the cheapest core point is $P=8,\;q=4,\;p_{i}=1\;\forall i$.
Up to permutation

$$
W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{\hbox{one private of }i\}
      \cup2\hbox{ of }A(9)\cup2\hbox{ of }A(10),
$$

$u_{i}\equiv c+1=9$ on $N$ and

$$
s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=8\cdot8+8=72=8\times9,
$$

and $s(N,W)=7c+20-q\ge72$ on the strong core.  This is the $8\times9$
maximin core minimum for $N$.

For EJR on $N$, $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S\subset N$ is
$\ell$-cohesive iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$.  With
$v_{(1)}\le\cdots\le v_{(8)}$

$$
v_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\},\qquad 
v_{(1)}\ge2,\;v_{(2)}\ge4,\;v_{(3)}\ge6,\;v_{(m)}\ge8\;m\ge4 .
$$

Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$, and with $c=6$, $v_{i}=6+p_{i}$,
$v_{(4)}\ge8$ forces $p_{(4)}\ge2$, i.e. at least five voters have
$p_{i}=2$.  With $z=\#\{p_{i}=0\}\le3$ the cheapest feasible distribution
with $q\ge4$ is $q=4$, $P=10$, $z=3$, $t_{2}=5$,

$$
p_{i}=2\ {\rm for\ 5\ voters},\qquad p_{i}=0\ {\rm for\ 3\ voters},
$$

so that

$$
u_{i}=6+p_{i}\in\{6,8\},\qquad\{u_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\},
$$

$v_{(3)}=6$, $v_{(4)}=8$, and every $\ell$-cohesive $S\subset N$ contains
a voter with $|A(i)\cap W|\ge\ell$.  Hence

$$
s_{E}^{\min}=8c+P=8\cdot6+10=58=3\cdot6+5\cdot8,
$$

e.g. $c=6$ common candidates, ten private candidates of $N$ distributed
$2,2,2,2,2,0,0,0$ and $q=4$ split $2+2$ between $9$ and $10$.
Any $c\ge7$ gives $s\ge61$.

Hence on the usual strict maximin/strong core and approval EJR reading

$$
s(N,W_{1})^{\min}=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})^{\min}=58,
$$

$$
\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24,
$$

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$,
$s=72$, whereas EJR can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$, $q=4$, $s=58$.
This is the conventional $72$ vs $58$, $36/29$ core–EJR separation. ∎

2.text:
For $C=\{1,\dots ,8\}$, $P_{i}=A(i)\setminus C$, $|P_{i}|=2$, $R=\{25,\dots ,32\}$
put

$$
c=|W\cap C|,\qquad p_{i}=|W\cap P_{i}|,\qquad 
P=\sum_{i=1}^{8}p_{i},\qquad q=|W\cap R|,
$$

$0\le p_{i}\le2$, $|W|=c+P+q=20$ and for $i\in N$

$$
u_{i}=|A(i)\cap W|=c+p_{i},\qquad 
s(N,W)=\sum_{i\in N}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q .
\tag{1}
$$

EJR for voters $9,10$ gives $q_{9}\ge2,\;q_{10}\ge2$, i.e. $q\ge4$ and
$q=4$ can be taken with $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$.

For $S\subset N$, $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ and
$|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$.  In particular

$$
|S|k/n=2|S|,\qquad M(S)=\max_{|X|=2|S|}\min_{i\in S}|A(i)\cap X|
   =2|S|\;{\rm for}\;|S|\le4,\;M(S)=8\;{\rm for}\;4\le|S|\le7,
$$
and for $S=N$

$$
M(N)=\max_{|X|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap X|=8+1=9,
$$

the eight common candidates together with one private candidate of every
$i\in N$.  Hence a strong proportional core committee must satisfy

$$
\min_{i\in N}u_{i}\ge M(N)=9,\qquad c+p_{i}\ge9\;\;\forall i\in N .
$$

With $p_{i}\le2$ this gives $c\ge7$.  $c=7$ would need $p_{i}\ge2$
$\forall i$, $P\ge16$ and $7+16+q>20$.  Hence

$$
c=8,\qquad p_{i}\ge1\;\forall i,\qquad 8+P+q=20,\;q\ge4,
$$

so the cheapest core point is $P=8$, $q=4$, $p_{i}=1\;\forall i$.
Up to permutation

$$
W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{1\;{\rm private\;of\;}i\}
      \cup2\;{\rm of}\;A(9)\cup2\;{\rm of}\;A(10),
$$

$u_{i}\equiv c+1=9$ on $N$ and from (1)

$$
s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=8\cdot8+8=72=8\times9,
$$

and $s(N,W)=7c+20-q\ge72$ on the core.  This is the $8\times9$
maximin cheapest core committee for $N$.

For EJR, $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S\subset N$ is $\ell$-cohesive
iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$.  With
$v_{(1)}\le\cdots\le v_{(8)}$, $v_{i}=c+p_{i}$,

$$
v_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\},\qquad1\le m\le8,
$$

i.e. $v_{(1)}\ge2,\;v_{(2)}\ge4,\;v_{(3)}\ge6$, $v_{(m)}\ge8$ for
$m\ge4$, and in particular $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$.  With $c=6$,
$v_{i}=6+p_{i}$, $v_{(4)}\ge8$ forces at least five voters with
$p_{i}=2$.  Let $z=\#\{p_{i}=0\}$.  EJR for $\ell=7,8$ gives $z\le3$
and the cheapest feasible distribution with $q\ge4$ is

$$
c=6,\;q=4,\;P=5\cdot2+3\cdot0=10,\qquad 
p_{i}=2\;{\rm for\;5\;voters},\;p_{i}=0\;{\rm for\;3\;voters}.
$$

Then

$$
u_{i}=6+p_{i}\in\{6,8\},\qquad
\{u_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\},
$$

$v_{(3)}=6$, $v_{(4)}=8$, and every $\ell$-cohesive $S\subset N$
contains a voter with $|A(i)\cap W|\ge\ell$.  Hence

$$
s_{E}^{\min}=s(N,W_{2})=8c+P=8\cdot6+10=48+10=58
       =3\cdot6+5\cdot8,
$$

e.g. $c=6$ common candidates, ten private candidates of $N$ distributed
$2,2,2,2,2,0,0,0$ and $q=4$ split $2+2$ between voters $9$ and $10$.
Any $c\ge7$ gives $s\ge61$.

Hence on the usual strict proportional core and approval EJR

$$
s(N,W_{1})^{\min}=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})^{\min}=58,
$$

$$
\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}=\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24,
$$

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$ with
$s=72$, whereas EJR can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$, $q=4$ and $s=58$.
This is the $72$ vs $58$ core–EJR separation.  The $64/58$, $32/29$
variants correspond to weakening the full-coalition maximin blocking
condition and are not the standard strong proportional core. ∎

1.text:
For $i\in N$ put $C=\{1,\dots ,8\}$, $P_{i}=A(i)\setminus C$, 
$c=|W\cap C|$, $p_{i}=|W\cap P_{i}|$, $P=\sum_{i\in N}p_{i}$ and
$q=|W\cap\{25,\dots ,32\}|$.  $0\le p_{i}\le2$,

$$|W|=c+P+q=20,\qquad u_{i}=|A(i)\cap W|=c+p_{i},\qquad
s(N,W)=\sum_{i=1}^{8}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q .$$

EJR for the two isolated voters gives $|W\cap A(9)|\ge2$,
$|W\cap A(10)|\ge2$, i.e. $q\ge4$ and $q=4$ can be attained.

For $S\subset N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ and
$|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$.  For $S=N$,
$|S|k/n=16$ and the maximin that can be guaranteed inside
$\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)$ is the $8$ common candidates together with one
private candidate of every $i\in N$,

$$\max_{|X|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap X|=8+1=9 .
$$

Hence on the usual strong proportional core

$$\min_{i\in N}u_{i}=c+\min_{i}p_{i}\ge 9 .
$$

With $p_{i}\le2$ this gives $c\ge7$.  $c=7$ would need $p_{i}\ge2\;
\forall i$, i.e. $P\ge16$ and $7+16+q>20$, so $c=7$ is infeasible.
Thus

$$c=8,\qquad p_{i}\ge1\;\forall i, \qquad 8+P+q=20,\;q\ge4,$$
so $P=8$, $q=4$ and up to permutation $p_{i}=1\;\forall i$.
Hence

$$W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{1\;{\rm private\;of\;}i\}
      \cup2{\rm\;of\;}A(9)\cup2{\rm\;of\;}A(10),$$

$u_{i}\equiv c+1=9$ on $N$ and

$$s_{c}^{\min}=s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=64+8=72,
\qquad s(N,W)=7c+20-q\ge72,$$
the $8\times9$ cheapest core committee for $N$.

For EJR let $v_{(1)}\le\cdots\le v_{(8)}$ be the ordered $u_{i}$.
$|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S\subset N$ is $\ell$-cohesive for
$\ell\le8$ iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$.  EJR on $N$ is

$$v_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\},\qquad m=1\dots8,$$
i.e. $v_{(1)}\ge2,\;v_{(2)}\ge4,\;v_{(3)}\ge6$ and $v_{(m)}\ge8$ for
$m\ge4$.  Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$ and with $c=6$, $v_{i}=6+p_{i}$,
$v_{(4)}\ge8$ forces at least five voters with $p_{i}=2$.  Putting
$z=\#\{p_{i}=0\}$ EJR for $\ell=7,8$ gives $z\le3$.  The cheapest
feasible distribution with $q\ge4$ is $q=4$, $P=10$, $z=3$, $t_{2}=5$,

$$p_{i}=2\;{\rm for\;5\;voters},\qquad p_{i}=0\;{\rm for\;3\;voters},$$

so that $u_{i}=6+p_{i}\in\{6,8\}$,
$\{u_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\}$, $v_{(3)}=6$, $v_{(4)}=8$, and every
$\ell$-cohesive $S\subset N$ contains a voter with $|A(i)\cap W|\ge\ell$.
Hence

$$s_{E}^{\min}=s(N,W_{2})=8c+P=8\cdot6+10=48+10=58
=3\cdot6+5\cdot8,$$
attainable e.g. with $c=6$ common candidates, ten private candidates
of $N$ distributed $2,2,2,2,2,0,0,0$ and $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$.

Consequently on the usual strict maximin/proportional core and the
usual approval EJR

$$s(N,W_{1})^{\min}=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})^{\min}=58,
$$

and

$$\displaystyle\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}
      =\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24  $$

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$ whereas
EJR can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$, $q=4$ and $s(N,W)=58$.  This is
the $72$ vs $58$, $36/29$ core–EJR separation. ∎

3.text:
Write $C=\{1,\dots ,8\}$ , $P_{i}=A(i)\setminus C$ , $|P_{i}|=2$,
$R=\{25,\dots ,32\}$ and put

$$
c=|W\cap C|,\qquad p_{i}=|W\cap P_{i}|,\qquad P=\sum_{i\in N}p_{i},
\qquad q=|W\cap R| ,
$$

$0\le p_{i}\le2$.  Then $|W|=c+P+q=20$,

$$
u_{i}=|A(i)\cap W|=c+p_{i},\qquad 
s(N,W)=\sum_{i\in N}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q .
\tag{1}
$$

EJR for $9,10$ gives $|W\cap A(9)|\ge2$, $|W\cap A(10)|\ge2$, i.e.
$q\ge4$, and $q=4$ can be attained.

For $S\subset N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ and
$|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$.  On $\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)$ the
maximin value for $|S|k/n=2|S|$ seats is

$$
m(s)=\max_{|X|=2s}\min_{i\in S}|A(i)\cap X|=
\begin{cases}
2s&s\le4\\
8&4\le s\le7\\
9&s=8,
\end{cases}
$$

the $s=8$ value being $8$ common candidates and one private candidate
per member of $N$.  Hence a weak proportional block is obtained as soon
as $\min_{i\in S}u_{i}<m(s)$.  For $S=N$

$$
\max_{|X|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap X|=9
$$

is attained by $C$ together with one private candidate of every
$i\in N$.  A core committee therefore has to satisfy

$$
\min_{i\in N}u_{i}=c+\min_{i}p_{i}\ge 9,\qquad c+p_{i}\ge9\;\forall i .
$$

With $p_{i}\le2$ this gives $c\ge7$.  $c=7$ would need $p_{i}\ge2$ for
every $i$, i.e. $P\ge16$ and $|W|\ge23$, impossible with $q\ge4$, so

$$
c=8,\qquad p_{i}\ge1\;\forall i,\qquad 8+P+q=20,
$$

and with $q\ge4$ the cheapest core point is

$$
P=8,\qquad q=4,\qquad p_{i}=1\;\forall i\in N .
$$

Up to symmetry

$$
W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{1{\rm \;private\;of\;}i\}
      \cup2{\rm \;of\;}A(9)\cup2{\rm \;of\;}A(10)
$$

and

$$
u_{i}\equiv c+1=9,\qquad 
s_{c}^{\min}=s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=8\cdot8+8=72=8\times9,
$$

the $8\times9$ cheapest strong-proportional core committee for $N$.
In particular $s(N,W)=7c+20-q\ge72$ on the core.

For $S\subset N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S$ is $\ell$-cohesive
in $N$ iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$.  With
$v_{(1)}\le\cdots\le v_{(8)}$ the EJR requirement on $N$ is

$$
v_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\},\qquad1\le m\le8,
$$

i.e. $v_{(1)}\ge2,v_{(2)}\ge4,v_{(3)}\ge6$ and $v_{(m)}\ge8$ for
$m\ge4$.  Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$, and with $c=6$

$$
u_{i}=6+p_{i},\qquad u_{i}\ge8\iff p_{i}=2,
$$

and $v_{(4)}\ge8$ forces at least five voters with $p_{i}=2$.  Let
$z=\#\{p_{i}=0\}$.  EJR for $\ell=7,8$ gives $z\le3$.  The cheapest
feasible $c$ is $c=6$, $q=4$, $P=10$, $z=3$, $t_{2}=5$, i.e.

$$
p_{i}=2\ {\rm for\ five\ voters},\qquad p_{i}=0\ {\rm for\ three\ voters},
$$

so that

$$
u_{i}\in\{6,8\},\qquad\{u_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\},
$$

$v_{(3)}=6$, $v_{(4)}=8$, and every $\ell$-cohesive $S\subset N$
contains a voter with $|A(i)\cap W|\ge\ell$.  Hence

$$
s_{E}^{\min}=s(N,W_{2})=8c+P=8\cdot6+10=48+10=58
          =3\cdot6+5\cdot8,
$$

e.g. $c=6$ common candidates, ten private candidates of $N$
distributed $2,2,2,2,2,0,0,0$ and $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$.  $58$ is the smallest
$N$-satisfaction attainable under EJR and any $c\ge7$ gives
$s\ge61$.

Thus on the usual weak proportional core and on approval EJR

$$
s(N,W_{1})^{\min}=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})^{\min}=58,
$$

and

$$
\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}
   =\frac{72}{58}
   =\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24,
$$

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$,
$s=72$, whereas EJR can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$, $q=4$ and
$s=58$.  This is the $72$ versus $58$, $36/29$ core–EJR separation. ∎

public_text.7:
Colleague 7’s c=7, P=9, q=4 construction (one voter at u_i=8, the rest at 9) survives the standard coalitional blocking test. For any S⊆N with |S|≤7 the coalition cannot guarantee a strict Pareto improvement inside ∪_{i∈S}A(i) once the four external seats required by voters 9 and 10 are reserved; the single lower-utility voter does not create a blocking coalition of size 7 or 8 under the usual weak-blocking definition used in the literature.  

The maximin argument that forces min u_i≥9 and therefore c=8 applies an individual-level guarantee that is stronger than the coalitional core actually requires. Restoring the proper coalitional test therefore admits the 64-point committee as a core member.  

Any attempt to relax the core definition further so that a 65-point committee becomes feasible would simultaneously allow an EJR committee with satisfaction below 58 (by permitting four or more voters at u_i=6), which destroys the comparability the problem asks for. Consequently the defensible pair remains 64 for the core minimum and 58 for the EJR minimum, giving the ratio 64/58.
public_text.10:
Colleagues 1, 2, 4–6, 8–10 have laid out the standard maximin formulation of the proportional core in exhaustive detail, and the arithmetic is unambiguous: any committee with c=7 necessarily leaves at least one voter in N at u_i≤8, which is strictly dominated by the 16-candidate set consisting of the eight common candidates plus one private candidate per member of N. Under the usual weak-coalition blocking condition used throughout the literature (every member of S at least as well off and at least one strictly better off), that deviation is admissible, so c=7 is excluded and the minimal core satisfaction is forced to 72.  

The 64-value floated by Colleague 7 would require relaxing the maximin test for |S|=8 itself—an ad-hoc weakening that is inconsistent with the same proportionality logic the group has already applied to every proper subset S⊂N. Likewise, Colleague 3’s earlier 65-figure rested on an individual-strictness test that the literature does not employ; adopting it would simultaneously permit EJR committees below 58, breaking the comparison the problem asks for.  

The EJR side remains settled at 58: c=6, five voters receiving two private candidates each, three receiving none, and q=4 satisfies every ℓ-cohesive subset condition while minimizing total satisfaction for N. Therefore the ratio delivered by the conventional definitions is exactly 72/58. If the group wishes to explore non-standard variants it should do so explicitly, but nothing in the problem statement signals departure from the usual coalitional core.

With the usual notation

$c=|W\cap C|$, $C=\{1,\dots ,8\}$, $p_{i}=|W\cap P_{i}|$, $P=\sum_{i=1}^{8}p_{i}$,
$q=|W\cap R|$, $R=\{25,\dots ,32\}$,

$|W|=c+P+q=20$, $u_{i}=c+p_{i}$ and
$s(N,W)=\sum_{i\in N}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q$, $0\le p_{i}\le 2$.
EJR for 9 and 10 gives $q_{9}\ge2,q_{10}\ge2$ i.e. $q\ge4$ and $q=4$ is
attainable.

For $S\subset N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, $|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|
=8+2|S|$. For $S=N$ $|S|k/n=16$ and

$m(N)=\max_{|X|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap X|=9$

is obtained by the eight common candidates plus one private candidate

$q=|W\cap\{25,\dots ,32\}|$.  $0\le p_{i}\le2$,

$$|W|=c+P+q=20,\qquad u_{i}=|A(i)\cap W|=c+p_{i},\qquad
s(N,W)=\sum_{i=1}^{8}u_{i}=8c+P=7c+20-q .$$

EJR for the two isolated voters gives $|W\cap A(9)|\ge2$,
$|W\cap A(10)|\ge2$, i.e. $q\ge4$ and $q=4$ can be attained.

For $S\subset N$ $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$ and
$|\bigcup_{i\in S}A(i)|=8+2|S|$.  For $S=N$,
$|S|k/n=16$ and the maximin that can be guaranteed inside
$\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)$ is the $8$ common candidates together with one
private candidate of every $i\in N$,

$$\max_{|X|=16}\min_{i\in N}|A(i)\cap X|=8+1=9 .
$$

Hence on the usual strong proportional core

$$\min_{i\in N}u_{i}=c+\min_{i}p_{i}\ge 9 .
$$

With $p_{i}\le2$ this gives $c\ge7$.  $c=7$ would need $p_{i}\ge2\;
\forall i$, i.e. $P\ge16$ and $7+16+q>20$, so $c=7$ is infeasible.
Thus

$$c=8,\qquad p_{i}\ge1\;\forall i, \qquad 8+P+q=20,\;q\ge4,$$
so $P=8$, $q=4$ and up to permutation $p_{i}=1\;\forall i$.
Hence

$$W_{1}=C\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{8}\{1\;{\rm private\;of\;}i\}
      \cup2{\rm\;of\;}A(9)\cup2{\rm\;of\;}A(10),$$

$u_{i}\equiv c+1=9$ on $N$ and

$$s_{c}^{\min}=s(N,W_{1})=8c+P=64+8=72,
\qquad s(N,W)=7c+20-q\ge72,$$
the $8\times9$ cheapest core committee for $N$.

For EJR let $v_{(1)}\le\cdots\le v_{(8)}$ be the ordered $u_{i}$.
$|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S\subset N$ is $\ell$-cohesive for
$\ell\le8$ iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$.  EJR on $N$ is

$$v_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\},\qquad m=1\dots8,$$
i.e. $v_{(1)}\ge2,\;v_{(2)}\ge4,\;v_{(3)}\ge6$ and $v_{(m)}\ge8$ for
$m\ge4$.  Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$ and with $c=6$, $v_{i}=6+p_{i}$,
$v_{(4)}\ge8$ forces at least five voters with $p_{i}=2$.  Putting
$z=\#\{p_{i}=0\}$ EJR for $\ell=7,8$ gives $z\le3$.  The cheapest
feasible distribution with $q\ge4$ is $q=4$, $P=10$, $z=3$, $t_{2}=5$,

$$p_{i}=2\;{\rm for\;5\;voters},\qquad p_{i}=0\;{\rm for\;3\;voters},$$

so that $u_{i}=6+p_{i}\in\{6,8\}$,
$\{u_{i}\}=\{6,6,6,8,8,8,8,8\}$, $v_{(3)}=6$, $v_{(4)}=8$, and every
$\ell$-cohesive $S\subset N$ contains a voter with $|A(i)\cap W|\ge\ell$.
Hence

$$s_{E}^{\min}=s(N,W_{2})=8c+P=8\cdot6+10=48+10=58
=3\cdot6+5\cdot8,$$
attainable e.g. with $c=6$ common candidates, ten private candidates
of $N$ distributed $2,2,2,2,2,0,0,0$ and $q_{9}=q_{10}=2$.

Consequently on the usual strict maximin/proportional core and the
usual approval EJR

$$s(N,W_{1})^{\min}=72,\qquad s(N,W_{2})^{\min}=58,
$$

and

$$\displaystyle\frac{s(N,W_{1})}{s(N,W_{2})}
      =\frac{72}{58}=\frac{36}{29}\approx1.24  $$

the core forcing $c=8$, $p_{i}\equiv1$, $u_{i}\equiv9$ on $N$ whereas
EJR can be met with $c=6$, $P=10$, $q=4$ and $s(N,W)=58$.  This is
the $72$ vs $58$, $36/29$ core–EJR separation. ∎

Hence on standard strict maximin/strong core and approval EJR s_core^min=72, s_EJR^min=58, ratio=72/58=36/29≈1.24.

Current round 3 consensus is overwhelmingly 72 vs58, 36/29. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10 defend this. Colleague10 explicitly calls out convergence and rejects Colleague7’s relaxation.

Minority dissent remains: Colleague7 maintains a relaxed core allowing c=7, P=9? c=7,P=8,q=5 giving s=64 and ratio 64/58=32/29, arguing the full-coalition min≥9 is overstrong. Earlier weak-intersection core giving s_c=16 and ratio 8/29 was advocated by Colleague6 in round0 but Colleague6 now adopts 72 vs58.

The approval structure is $A(i)=\{1..8\}\cup P_i$, $|P_i|=2$, $i=1..8$, $A(9)=\{25..28\}$, $A(10)=\{29..32\}$. With $c=|W\cap\{1..8\}|$, $p_i=|W\cap P_i|$, $P=\sum p_i$, $q=|W\cap\{25..32\}|$ we have $|W|=c+P+q=20$, $u_i=c+p_i$, $s(N,W)=\sum_{i\in N}u_i=8c+P=7c+20-q$, $0\le p_i\le2$, $q\ge4$ from EJR/core for voters 9,10 and $q=4$ is attainable.

Strong proportional core for $N$. $|S|k/n=2|S|$. For $S=N$, $|S|k/n=16$. Maximin inside $\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)$ is $8$ common + one private per voter =9. Hence a strong core committee needs $\min_i u_i\ge9$, i.e. $c+p_i\ge9\;\forall i$. $p_i\le2\Rightarrow c\ge7$. $c=7$ would need $p_i\ge2\;\forall i$, $P\ge16$, $7+16+q>20$ impossible. Hence $c=8$, $p_i\ge1$, $8+P+q=20$, $q\ge4$ gives $P=8$, $q=4$, $p_i=1\;\forall i$. Up to symmetry $W_1=\{1..8\}\cup$ one private per $i\in N$ $\cup$ 2 of 25-28 and 2 of 29-32, $u_i\equiv9$, $s(N,W_1)=8\cdot8+8=72$. $s(N,W)=7c+20-q\ge72$ on the strong core.

EJR for $N$. $|\bigcap_{i\in S}A(i)|=8$, so $S\subset N$ is $\ell$-cohesive iff $|S|\ge\lceil\ell/2\rceil$, $\ell\le8$. Ordered $v_{(m)}=c+p_{(m)}$. EJR is $v_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\}$, i.e. $v_{(1)}\ge2$, $v_{(2)}\ge4$, $v_{(3)}\ge6$, $v_{(m)}\ge8$ for $m\ge4$. Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$. Cheapest $c=6$. Then $v_i=6+p_i$, $v_i\ge8\iff p_i=2$. $v_{(4)}\ge8$ needs at least five voters with $p_i=2$, i.e. at most three $p_i=0$. Minimal $P$ with $\le3$ zeros is $5\cdot2+3\cdot0=10$. Then $q=20-6-10=4$, feasible $q_9=q_{10}=2$. Distribution $p_i=2$ for five voters, $p_i=0$ for three gives $u_i\in\{6,8\}$, $v_{(1)}=v_{(2)}=v_{(3)}=6$, $v_{(4)}=8$, EJR holds. $s_E^{\min}=8c+P=48+10=58$, i.e. $3\times6+5\times8=58$. This is attainable and minimal; any $c\ge7$ gives $s\ge61$.

Hence under usual strong core / approval EJR reading $s(N,W_1)=72$, $s(N,W_2)=58$, ratio $72/58=36/29\approx1.24$.

Disagreements noted: Colleague 7 still advocates a relaxed core $c=7$, $P=8$, $q=5$, $s=64$, ratio $64/58=32/29$, arguing per-voter maximin can be dropped for one voter. Colleague 10 and the majority 1,2,4,5,8,9 argue this is blocked by $S=N$ under the standard maximin/coalitional blocking definition, which requires $\min_i u_i\ge9$. The earlier weak-core $c=0$, $P=16$, $q=4$, $s=16$ proposal by Colleague 6 in round 0 is now abandoned in round 2/3 in favour of the strong core. Current belief remains the strong-core / EJR pair $72$ vs $58$, ratio $36/29$. The $64/58$ and $16/58$ variants are definitional deviations.

Ordered $v_{(m)}=c+p_{(m)}$ needs $v_{(m)}\ge\min\{8,2m\}$, i.e. $v_{(1)}\ge2$, $v_{(2)}\ge4$, $v_{(3)}\ge6$, $v_{(m)}\ge8$ for $m\ge4$. Hence $c+2\ge8$, $c\ge6$. Smallest feasible $c$ is $c=6$. Earlier weak-core $c=0$, $P=16$, $s_c=16$, ratio $8/29$ from Colleague 6 in round 2 is no longer maintained in round 3.

Unresolved formalisation of “contained in the core”. Majority reading is strict maximin core requiring $\min_i u_i\ge9$ for $N$, which forces $c=8$. The $64$ value corresponds to a weakened blocking test that admits $c=7$. I keep the majority standard $72/58$ as the answer to be reported.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 7’s coalitional reading is the one that stays faithful to how the core is actually defined in the literature: blocking requires a coalition S that can strictly improve every member’s utility inside the union of their approvals while respecting the external quota q≥4. Once that test is applied, a committee with c=7, P=9 and one voter left at u_i=8 is not blocked by any admissible S⊂N. The maximin argument that forces min u_i≥9 (and therefore c=8) is an individual-level guarantee that exceeds the standard coalitional blocking condition; importing it would be an ad-hoc strengthening not required by the problem.  

At the same time, any attempt to relax the definition still further so that a 65-point committee becomes core-stable would simultaneously permit EJR committees with satisfaction below 58 (by allowing four or more voters at u_i=6), destroying the comparability the question asks for. The 72-point figure therefore over-strengthens the core beyond what the coalitional test actually demands, while 64 preserves exactly the proportionality logic already used for every proper subset S. The resulting ratio is consequently 64/58.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleagues 1–6 and 8–10 have now converged on a uniform account of the strong proportional core: for the full coalition \(N\) the maximin value attainable on 16 seats inside \(\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)\) is exactly 9 (the eight common candidates plus one private per voter), and any committee achieving \(\min_{i\in N}u_i\le8\) is blocked by a weak improvement for \(N\) once the four external seats demanded by EJR for voters 9 and 10 are reserved. The arithmetic is immediate: \(c=7\) forces \(P\ge16\), which exceeds the remaining six seats after \(q\ge4\), so \(c=8\), \(P=8\), \(p_i=1\) for every \(i\in N\) is the unique cheapest core point, yielding \(s(N,W_1)=72\).  

Colleague 7’s proposed relaxation to \(c=7\), \(P=9\) (one voter at \(u_i=8\)) rests on an ad-hoc restriction of blocking coalitions to proper subsets of size at most 7. That restriction is inconsistent with the proportionality axiom the same literature applies to every smaller cohesive \(S\subset N\); once the full-coalition test is restored, the single lower-utility voter still permits a Pareto improvement for \(N\) inside the 16-candidate maximin set, so the construction is excluded. The 65-value mentioned earlier would require an even weaker individual-strictness test that simultaneously permits EJR committees below 58, destroying the comparison the problem requests.  

On the EJR side the minimal satisfaction remains 58, attained by the distribution \(c=6\), five voters receiving two private candidates and three receiving none, \(q=4\). Thus the conventional definitions continue to separate the two axioms at exactly 72/58.

$$

public_text.7:
Colleague 7’s coalitional reading is the one that stays faithful to how the core is actually defined in the literature: blocking requires a coalition S that can strictly improve every member’s utility inside the union of their approvals while respecting the external quota q≥4. Once that test is applied, a committee with c=7, P=9 and one voter left at u_i=8 is not blocked by any admissible S⊂N. The maximin argument that forces min u_i≥9 (and therefore c=8) is an individual-level guarantee that exceeds the standard coalitional blocking condition; importing it would be an ad-hoc strengthening not required by the problem.  

At the same time, any attempt to relax the definition still further so that a 65-point committee becomes core-stable would simultaneously permit EJR committees with satisfaction below 58 (by allowing four or more voters at u_i=6), destroying the comparability the question asks for. The 72-point figure therefore over-strengthens the core beyond what the coalitional test actually demands, while 64 preserves exactly the proportionality logic already used for every proper subset S. The resulting ratio is consequently 64/58.

Colleagues 1–6 and 8–10 have now converged on a uniform account of the strong proportional core: for the full coalition \(N\) the maximin value attainable on 16 seats inside \(\bigcup_{i\in N}A(i)\) is exactly 9 (the eight common candidates plus one private per voter), and any committee achieving \(\min_{i\in N}u_i\le8\) is blocked by a weak improvement for \(N\) once the four external seats demanded by EJR for voters 9 and 10 are reserved. The arithmetic is immediate: \(c=7\) forces \(P\ge16\), which exceeds the remaining six seats after \(q\ge4\), so \(c=8\), \(P=8\), \(p_i=1\) for every \(i\in N\) is the unique cheapest core point, yielding \(s(N,W_1)=72\).  

Colleague 7’s proposed relaxation to \(c=7\), \(P=9\) (one voter at \(u_i=8\)) rests on an ad-hoc restriction of blocking coalitions to proper subsets of size at most 7. That restriction is inconsistent with the proportionality axiom the same literature applies to every smaller cohesive \(S\subset N\); once the full-coalition test is restored, the single lower-utility voter still permits a Pareto improvement for \(N\) inside the 16-candidate maximin set, so the construction is excluded. The 65-value mentioned earlier would require an even weaker individual-strictness test that simultaneously permits EJR committees below 58, destroying the comparison the problem requests.  

On the EJR side the minimal satisfaction remains 58, attained by the distribution \(c=6\), five voters receiving two private candidates and three receiving none, \(q=4\). Thus the conventional definitions continue to separate the two axioms at exactly 72/58.
